rabat: Rabat stands on Morocco's northwestern Atlantic coast, at the mouth of the river Bou Regreg, opposite Salé, the city's main commuter town. The name comes from the Arabic ar-Ribat, a ribat being an Islamic base or fortification. It is short for Ribat al-Fath, the ribat of conquest or stronghold of victory, a title given by the Almohads when they established the city as a naval base in 1170. The oldest part of the present city is the Kasbah of the Udayas, built by the Almohads in the 12th century.

In the first millennium BCE the Phoenicians founded trading colonies along the Atlantic coast, although archaeologists have debated whether a Phoenician settlement called Sala existed here. By the first century BCE the region had come under the influence of Rome, which annexed the Mauretanian Kingdom and built a city called Sala Colonia at the site now known as Chellah, just south of the walled city. With Lixus it was one of the two main Roman naval outposts on the Atlantic coast of Mauretania Tingitana. In the 10th century the Umayyads of Córdoba, or their Zenata Berber allies, founded a ribat in the area against the Barghawata Berbers.

In 1609 Philip III decreed the expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain. About 2,000 refugees from Hornachos settled around Salé and occupied the kasbah, and Rabat and Salé united in 1627 to form the Republic of Bou Regreg, a base for corsairs known as the Salé Rovers. Al-Rashid, founder of the 'Alawi dynasty, conquered the area in 1666, though the sultans allowed piracy to continue until the early 19th century, and Austria shelled the city in 1829 after losing a ship to a pirate attack.

After the Treaty of Fes established the French protectorate in March 1912, General Hubert Lyautey moved the capital from Fez to Rabat. He argued that its coast was pleasanter and more accessible and that it lay close to Casablanca, which he expected to become the main economic centre. In 1913 he hired Henri Prost to design the Ville Nouvelle as an administrative sector. Rabat became the capital of independent Morocco in 1956.

Rabat is the capital of Morocco and one of the country's four imperial cities, and its medina is a World Heritage Site. The Kasbah of the Udayas is a residential district of white and blue houses and contains the Old Mosque, founded in 1150 and largely restored in the 18th century. The Oudayas Museum, in a pavilion built by Sultan Moulay Isma'il, opened in 1915 and is one of the oldest public museums in Morocco. The city hosts the headquarters of several international and African organisations, and Mohammed V University was founded there in 1957.
rabindranath-tagore: Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861 in the Jorasanko mansion in Calcutta, the youngest of 13 surviving children of Debendranath Tagore and Sarada Devi. His mother died in his early childhood, and he was raised mostly by servants. The family was at the forefront of the Bengal Renaissance, hosting literary magazines, theatre and recitals of Bengali and Western classical music. Tagore wrote poetry at eight, and at sixteen published poems under the pseudonym Bhanusimha that literary authorities took for long-lost classics.

Tagore wrote novels, essays, short stories, travelogues, dramas and thousands of songs. He is credited with originating the Bengali short story. Gitanjali, Gora and Ghare-Baire are his best-known works, and his compositions became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. In 1912 he took translations of his works to England, where William Butler Yeats, who wrote the preface to the English Gitanjali, and others noticed them.

He opposed imperialism and supported Indian nationalists, yet he rebuked strongly nationalist forms of the independence movement. In 1925 he attacked the Swadeshi movement in an essay, The Cult of the Charkha. He urged the masses to seek self-help and education rather than blind revolution, and his religious and philosophical ideas appear in the 1922 lectures Creative Unity and the 1931 Hibbert Lectures at Oxford, published as The Religion of Man.

Tagore conceived a new kind of university to make Santiniketan a connecting thread between India and the world. He named it Visva-Bharati; its foundation stone was laid on 24 December 1918, and teaching was often done under trees. He died on 7 August 1941 at Jorasanko Thakur Bari, the house in which he was born.
rajasthan: Rajasthan covers 342,239 square kilometres, about 10.4 per cent of India's area, and includes most of the wide and inhospitable Thar Desert, also called the Great Indian Desert. The Aravalli Range runs through the state from south-west to north-east for more than 850 kilometres, with Mount Abu, the state's only hill station, at its south-western end. About three fifths of the state lies north-west of the range. It borders the Pakistani provinces of Punjab and Sindh and five Indian states. The name means Land of Kings, from the Sanskrit rājā and sthāna. It first appears in print in the 1829 Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, and Rajputana, the earlier name for the region, appears in George Thomas's memoir of 1800.

Parts of the area belonged to the Vedic and Indus Valley civilisations. Kalibangan, in Hanumangarh district, was a major provincial capital of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and a settlement at Balathal, in Udaipur district, dates from 3000 to 1500 BCE. Stone Age tools between 5,000 and 200,000 years old have been found in Bundi and Bhilwara districts. The Rajputs, according to Topsfield, entered India from the north-west in the first millennium CE and set up kingdoms in what is now Rajasthan. The Pratiharas, with their seat at Kannauj, were acknowledged by almost all of North India up to the 10th century.

In 1178 a confederacy of Rajputs under Mularaja II of the Kingdom of Gujarat defeated the Ghurids at the Battle of Kasahrada. Prithviraj Chauhan led a confederacy of Rajput clans that defeated Muhammad Ghori at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191, but Ghori decisively defeated him at the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192, and part of Rajasthan then came under Muslim rulers, with centres at Nagaur and Ajmer. At the beginning of the 13th century Mewar was the most powerful state of the region. The Rajputs resisted the Muslim incursions from the 13th century onwards and preserved Hindu culture at their courts.

The modern state was formed from the states of the Rajputana Agency of British India, which merged into the Indian Union. It includes most of Rajputana: nineteen princely states, three chiefships and the British district of Ajmer-Merwara. Jaisalmer, Marwar (Jodhpur), Bikaner, Mewar (Chittorgarh), Alwar and Dhundhar (Jaipur) were among the main Rajput states, Bharatpur and Dholpur were Jat states, and Tonk was ruled by Pathans.

Rajasthan is a state of India with its capital and largest city at Jaipur. Its main features include the Indus Valley ruins at Kalibangan, the Jain pilgrimage site of the Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu and Keoladeo National Park at Bharatpur, a World Heritage Site known for its birds.
rama: The word Rama is Vedic Sanskrit with two contextual meanings. In the Atharva Veda it means dark or black, and in other Vedic texts pleasing, delightful or beautiful. The primary source of his life is the Sanskrit epic Ramayana, composed by the sage Valmiki, which exists in many versions across the regions of India.

Some Hindu texts place Rama in the Treta Yuga, which their authors estimate to have existed before about 5000 BCE. The archaeologist H. D. Sankalia calls this estimate pure speculation and suggests that the incidents of the story could have taken place between 1,500 and 700 BCE. Jain and Buddhist texts also tell the story, calling him Pauma or Padma in Jain accounts, with details that differ from the Hindu versions.

According to Valmiki, Rama was born in Ayodhya, capital of Kosala, to Dasaratha and his first wife Kausalya, and had the half-brothers Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna. He married Sita and spent fourteen years in forest exile, during which Sita was kidnapped by the demon-king Ravana. After the war he returned to Ayodhya and was crowned, and his rule, Rama rajya, is described as just and fair. Many believe that people lit lamps for his return, which links the festival of Diwali with him.

Hindus hold Rama to be a complete avatar of Vishnu, and some regard him as the ultimate Brahman. He is also viewed as the ideal man. By Hindu belief this avatar does not display Vishnu's divine powers and lives as a human. Scholars such as Paula Richman note that there are hundreds of versions of his story, none the single original, each valid in its local tradition.

The Ramayana has been retold in most major Indian languages, among them Kambar's Tamil Ramavataram in the 12th century, Krittibas Ojha's Bengali version in the 15th and Tulsidas's Awadhi Ramacharitamanasa in the 16th. Kalidasa's Raghuvamsa suggests that the legend was well established by the 4th or 5th century CE. The Ramanandi Sampradaya, founded by the 14th-century poet-saint Ramananda, became the largest Hindu monastic community in modern times.

The story arrived in Southeast Asia in the 1st millennium CE, and its influence grew in Java, Bali, Malaya, Burma, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos. It inspired Madhubani and Rajput paintings and the Ramlila performances held each autumn.
ramadan: Muslims hold that the Quran was revealed during Ramadan, and that Muhammad received his first revelation on Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, generally believed to be an odd-numbered night in the last ten days of the month. They also hold that all earlier scriptures were revealed in this month. They were first commanded to fast in the second year of the Hijra, 624 CE, but believe that fasting has always been necessary for believers to attain fear of God. Philip Jenkins argues that the fast grew out of the strict Lenten discipline of the Syrian Churches, a view other scholars share and some Muslim academics dispute.

The Islamic calendar is lunar, and each month begins when the first crescent of the new moon is sighted. Since the calendar has no intercalation, Ramadan migrates through the seasons. It lasts 29 or 30 days. Many Muslims insist on a local sighting of the moon to mark the start, while others use the calculated time of the new moon or the declaration of Saudi Arabia, so dates differ between countries, usually by a day.

Fasting from dawn to sunset is obligatory for Muslims who have reached puberty and are not ill, travelling, elderly, breastfeeding, pregnant or menstruating. The predawn meal is the suhur and the meal that breaks the fast at sunset is the iftar, traditionally opened with dates in memory of Muhammad's practice. Muslims also abstain from sinful speech, devote more time to prayer and charity, and are encouraged to read the whole Quran over the month. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, declared after the crescent of the next month is sighted or after 30 days of fasting.

Customs of the month vary widely. In some Islamic countries lanterns are strung up in public squares, a tradition believed to have originated under the Fatimid Caliphate, when the rule of Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah was acclaimed by people holding lanterns. In the Middle East a mesaharati beats a drum through the neighbourhood to wake people for suhur. In Shia Islam the 19th to 21st days of the month are marked in mourning for Ali, the fourth Rashidun caliph, who was struck during morning prayer on the 19th day in 40 AH and died on the 21st. In the USSR the practice of Ramadan was suppressed by officials, and in Albania Ramadan festivities were banned during the communist period, though many Albanians fasted in secret.
ramayana: The Ramayana is a Hindu smriti epic poem, traditionally attributed to Valmiki, and one of the two Itihasas, narratives of past events interspersed with teachings on the goals of human life; the other is the Mahabharata. Its name means Rama's journey. Scholars place the oral composition of its core before the rise of Buddhism, since the narrative does not mention Buddhism and names Ayodhya as the capital of Kosala rather than by the later name Saketa. Later stages of the text extend over centuries. Two major regional recensions, the northern and the southern, descend from a common oral source; the southern is more archaic and is the backbone of modern critical editions.

In its extant form the poem has over 24,000 couplet verses, called shlokas, in seven kāṇḍas, or books. Rāma, prince of Ayodhya and son of King Daśaratha, is to be crowned, but Kaikeyī, provoked by the maidservant Mantharā, demands that Rāma be exiled for fourteen years while her son Bharata succeeds. Sītā and his brother Lakṣmaṇa follow him into the forest.

Rāvaṇa, the king of Lanka, carries off Sītā. Rāma allies himself with the vānaras, among them Hanumān, who becomes his biggest devotee. Hanumān leaps across the sea to Lanka to find Sītā, and the army crosses over a bridge built by the vānaras Nala and Nīla. In the war that follows Rāma defeats Rāvaṇa, and he returns to Ayodhya with Sītā to be crowned.

The Ramayana strongly influenced later Sanskrit poetry and Hindu life and culture, and its moral influence includes the ideal of Rāmarājya, a state in which Rama is king. Diwali marks Rama's return to Ayodhya. There are many other versions, including Buddhist and Jain adaptations. Kamban wrote the Tamil Ramavataram in the 12th century. In Cambodia the Reamker is a national epic; the earliest mention of its manuscript is a 7th-century inscription, and the surviving text dates from the 16th century.
ranoji-scindia: Ranoji Scindia, also known as Ranoji Sendrak, was born about 1700 into a Maratha family. His father, Jankoji Rao I, was hereditary patil, or village head, of Kanherkhed, a village in the present Satara district of Maharashtra. In earlier centuries his forefathers had served as shiledars, cavalrymen, under the Bahmani Sultanate, and had held jagirs. As a young man he entered the service of Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath. Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar, one of the Peshwa's diplomats, recognised his talents and had him made personal bodyguard to the Peshwa's son, Baji Rao I.

When Baji Rao was appointed Peshwa at the age of twenty by Chhatrapati Shahu, the appointment aroused the jealousy of senior officials at the Maratha court. He therefore promoted talented young men, barely out of their teens, to command his troops, among them Ranoji Scindia, Malhar Rao Holkar, the Pawar brothers, Pilaji Jadhav and Fateh Singh Bhosle. None of them came from families that had held hereditary deshmukhi rights under earlier rulers such as the Deccan Sultanates.

Ranoji was in charge of the Maratha campaign that Baji Rao began in Malwa in 1726, and after it he established his capital at Ujjain in 1731. He appointed Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar as his dewan, or administrator, and Yashaji Rambhaji as commander of his army, and himself spent most of his life on campaign. Some historians credit him with bringing the Kumbh Mela to Ujjain in 1732.

Ranoji died on 3 July 1745. He had five sons: Jayappa Rao, Jyotiba Rao, Dattaji Rao, Tukoji Rao and Mahadji. The four eldest died in battles in northern India between 1750 and 1761. The dynasty went on to dominate central and northern India in the later 18th century through its presence at Delhi, its collection of chauth from neighbouring rulers and a modernised army, and his descendants ruled the princely state of Gwalior under the British.
raphael: Raphael was born in Urbino, a small city of the Papal States whose court had been established by Federico da Montefeltro, created Duke of Urbino by Pope Sixtus IV. His father, Giovanni Santi, was court painter to the Duke and also a poet who wrote a rhymed chronicle of Federico's life. Raphael's mother Màgia died in 1491, and his father on 1 August 1494, so that he was an orphan at eleven. His guardian became his uncle Bartolomeo, a priest, who engaged in litigation with his stepmother. Raphael probably took part in managing his father's workshop from a very early age.

He probably trained in the workshop of Pietro Perugino and was described as a fully trained master by 1500. From about 1504 he spent a good deal of time in Florence, though possibly never as a continuous resident. A letter of recommendation of October 1504 describes him as a young painter who had decided to study there.

In 1508 Raphael moved to Rome, where he lived for the rest of his life. Pope Julius II invited him, perhaps at the suggestion of the architect Donato Bramante, who came from just outside Urbino and was distantly related to him. Julius at once commissioned him to fresco what was meant to become the Pope's private library in the Vatican Palace, a far larger commission than any he had had before. The Raphael Rooms, with The School of Athens in the Stanza della Segnatura, became the largest work of his career.

According to Vasari, Raphael eventually had a workshop of fifty pupils and assistants, arguably the largest team under any single old master painter. The most important were Giulio Romano and Gianfrancesco Penni, who were left many of his drawings and continued the workshop after his death. In 1514 he became engaged to Maria Bibbiena, Cardinal Bibbiena's niece, but the marriage had not taken place when she died in 1520.

Raphael was one of the finest draftsmen in the history of Western art and used drawings extensively to plan his compositions; over four hundred sheets survive. He made no prints himself but collaborated with Marcantonio Raimondi on about fifty engravings, which were the main way his art was experienced outside Italy until the twentieth century. His influence in his own century was less than that of Michelangelo, but those who disliked the excesses of Mannerism soon held him up as the ideal balanced painter. In the 18th and 19th centuries his serene and harmonious qualities were again regarded as the highest models.
rashid-ali-al-gaylani: Rashid Ali was the son of Sayyid Abd al-Wahhab al-Gailani and belonged to a prominent Baghdad family whose name points to an origin in Gilan in Iran and which traces its ancestry to the Prophet Muhammad; he also descended from Circassian governors of the Ottoman period. He studied at the law school in Baghdad and practised as a lawyer before entering politics.

In 1924 Yasin al-Hashimi made him minister of justice in his first government, and he was elected president of the Chamber of Deputies in 1925 and 1926. Both men were nationalists opposed to any British part in Iraq's internal politics. They rejected the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty signed by the government of Nuri as-Said in 1930 and formed the Party of National Brotherhood. Gaylani was prime minister for the first time from March to November 1933.

He returned to the premiership on 31 March 1940, after the early death of King Ghazi, when Emir Abdul-Illah was regent for the four-year-old Faisal II. Gaylani refused Allied troops passage through Iraq, rejected calls to break with Fascist Italy and sent his justice minister, Naji Shawkat, to Ankara, where on 5 July 1940 he met the German ambassador, Franz von Papen. Britain imposed economic sanctions, and under pressure from the regent he resigned on 31 January 1941.

With the Golden Square he then planned to assassinate the regent, who discovered the plot on 31 March and fled. The coup followed on 1 April, and on 3 April a National Defence Government took office under Gaylani. He sent artillery against the RAF base at Habbaniya. On 2 May the base's commander struck first at the Iraqi positions; within a week the Iraqis left the escarpment, and British forces advanced through Fallujah on Baghdad. Gaylani fled to Iran on 30 May. An armistice was signed the next day, and the regent returned on 1 June. Immediately afterwards the Farhud, a violent pogrom against Jews, took place in Baghdad.

After British and Soviet forces invaded Iran on 25 August 1941 he went on to Italy and then Berlin, where Adolf Hitler received him and he was recognised as leader of an Iraqi government in exile. On Germany's defeat he found refuge in Saudi Arabia. He returned to Iraq only after the revolution of 1958 that overthrew the monarchy, plotted a revolt against the government of Abdul Karim Kassem and was sentenced to death. Pardoned in July 1961, he lived in Lebanon, where he died on 28 August 1965 at the age of 72.
recife: Recife stands on the northeastern Atlantic coast of Brazil, at the confluence of the Beberibe and Capibaribe rivers before they drain into the South Atlantic. The city is formed by three islands, Recife, Santo Antônio and Boa Vista, with other rivers including the Jiquiá, Tejipió, Jordão and Pina. More than 50 bridges link them, and the city is often called the Venice of Brazil. Its name alludes to the stone reefs that lie offshore. The climate is tropical monsoon, warm to hot with high humidity throughout the year, relieved by trade winds from the ocean.

Recife began as a collection of fishing shacks, inns and warehouses on the delta between the two rivers, in the captaincy of Pernambuco, sometime between 1535 and 1537, in the earliest days of Portuguese colonisation of the land later called Brazil. It was a settlement of fishermen and a way station for Portuguese sailors and passing ships. It became the main harbour of the Captaincy of Pernambuco, known for its large-scale production of sugar cane.

Portuguese rule lasted from the founding to 1630. The Dutch West India Company then held the city from 1630 to 1654, when it was known as Mauritsstad and served as the capital of the colony of New Holland in Dutch Brazil. Portuguese rule resumed in 1654 and continued through the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves (1815 to 1822), the Empire of Brazil (1822 to 1889) and the Republic of Brazil from 1889. Many places of significance in the city date to both the Portuguese and Dutch periods. Football in Pernambuco began in 1902, when English and Dutch sailors landed at Recife and played a game on the beach.

Recife is the capital of the state of Pernambuco and its largest city, with 1,488,920 residents at the 2022 census and a metropolitan population of 3,726,974. It is a major seaport and the most important commercial hub of the north and northeast of Brazil. The Federal University of Pernambuco is the largest university in the state. The Historic Centre of Olinda, 7 kilometres to the north, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, and the carnivals of Recife and Olinda are nationally known. Frevo and maracatu are characteristic music and dance of the region.
red-sea: The Red Sea is a mediterranean sea lying between the Arabian Peninsula and Africa, an inlet of the Indian Ocean. It connects to the ocean in the south through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden. To the north lie the Sinai Peninsula, the Gulf of Aqaba and the Gulf of Suez, which leads to the Suez Canal. It is about 2,250 km long and 355 km across at its widest point, with an average depth of 490 m and a maximum of 2,730 m in the central Suakin Trough.

The sea lies over the Red Sea Rift, part of the Great Rift Valley. It formed as the Arabian Peninsula split from the Horn of Africa, a movement that began in the Eocene and accelerated in the Oligocene. The sea is still widening and is considered likely to become an ocean in time. With high evaporation, little rain and no significant rivers draining into it, it is one of the saltiest bodies of water in the world.

The earliest known exploration was by the ancient Egyptians, who sought commercial routes to Punt. One such expedition took place around 2500 BCE and another around 1500 BCE, under Hatshepsut. The Book of Exodus tells of the Israelites crossing a sea that the Hebrew text calls Yam Suph, traditionally identified as the Red Sea; Rabbi Saadia Gaon (882 to 942 CE) placed the crossing at the Gulf of Suez.

In the Middle Ages the sea formed an important part of the spice trade route. In 1183 Raynald of Châtillon launched a raid down the sea against Muslim pilgrim convoys, causing fury across the Muslim world, although his target appears to have been the lightly armed convoys rather than the cities of Mecca and Medina. The opening of the Suez Canal in November 1869 let more than a thousand marine species of the Red Sea migrate northward into the Mediterranean.

Six countries border the Red Sea proper: Saudi Arabia and Yemen on the eastern shore, and Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Djibouti on the western. The Gulf of Suez lies wholly within Egypt, while the Gulf of Aqaba borders Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Ships passing between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean shorten the route between Asia and Europe by almost half compared with sailing round Africa. Its shallow shelves hold coral reefs, and more than 1,200 fish species have been recorded, about 10 per cent of them found nowhere else.
reggio-calabria: The history of the area before the Greeks arrived in the eighth century BCE is not reliably known. Mythical accounts name a series of peoples there, among them the Osci, Trojans, Oenotrians, Ligures, Ausones and Sicels, and say the land was first called Saturnia or Neptunia.

The name Italia first referred to the area around Reggio before it spread to southern Calabria and, around the third century BCE, to the whole peninsula. By tradition it comes from Italus, an Oenotrian king. The city has borne many names: Rhegion in Greek times, briefly Phoibeia under Dionysius II of Syracuse, Regium or Rhegium in Latin, Rhegium Julii under the empire, Riyyu under the Emirate of Sicily and Rìsa under the Normans.

In the 5th and 6th centuries the Vandals, Lombards and Goths invaded. Under Byzantine rule Reggio became a metropolis of the Byzantine possessions in Italy and several times the capital of the Duchy of Calabria between 536 and 1060. Spanish Habsburg viceroys governed it from 1504 to 1713.

The 16th and 17th centuries brought decay through taxes, plague, the earthquake of 1562 and Ottoman raids: in 1534 the townspeople fled a fleet under Hayreddin Barbarossa, who captured eight hundred who remained and burned the town, and Barbary pirates took most of the inhabitants as slaves to Tripoli after an attack in 1558. On 21 August 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi took the city from the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

Reggio lies near the fault line where the Eurasian and African plates meet along the Strait of Messina, and earthquakes have destroyed it several times: in 91 BCE, after which Augustus ordered its reconstruction, then in 17 CE, 305, 374, 1562, 1783 and 1908. The quake of 1562 destroyed the medieval port and submerged the promontory of Calamizzi, where the first Greek settlers had landed. The 1783 and 1908 disasters, the second the worst natural calamity in Europe in human memory, produced the present layout of straight, intersecting streets, planned by Giovanbattista Mori in 1784 and Pietro de Nava in 1911.

Reggio Calabria is the largest city of Calabria, on the toe of the Italian peninsula opposite Sicily, with a population of 167,925. Its National Archaeological Museum of Magna Graecia houses the Bronzes of Riace, which have given it the nickname City of Bronzes. It is also called the City of bergamot, which is cultivated only in the region. Travellers who visited it include Pieter Bruegel around 1550, Stendhal in 1817, Edward Lear in 1847 and D. H. Lawrence around 1920.
reims: Before the Roman conquest of northern Gaul, Reims was the capital of the Remi tribe, founded about 80 BCE. In Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul the Remi allied themselves with the Romans and secured the special favour of the imperial power. Christianity was established there by 260, when Saint Sixtus of Reims founded the diocese. The Vandals captured the city in 406 and killed Bishop Nicasius, and in 451 Attila the Hun put it to fire and sword.

Remigius, bishop of Reims, baptised Clovis, King of the Salian Franks, with oil from a sacred phial said to have been brought from heaven by a dove. For centuries the monarchy used the event as a symbol of the divine right to rule. Archbishop Adalberon, with the monk Gerbert, later Pope Silvester II, founded schools in the 10th century that taught the liberal arts. The archbishops held the right to consecrate the kings of France, which they exercised, with few exceptions, from Philippe II Augustus, anointed in 1179, to Charles X, anointed in 1825.

In 1429 Joan of Arc had Charles VII consecrated in the cathedral. In the First World War German bombardment and fire in 1914 severely damaged the cathedral. On 7 May 1945 General Eisenhower and the Allies received the unconditional surrender of the German Wehrmacht at Reims, signed by General Alfred Jodl.

Reims is the most populous city of the department of Marne, 129 kilometres north-east of Paris on the Vesle river. Reims Cathedral, the adjacent Palace of Tau and the Abbey of Saint-Remi were listed together as a World Heritage Site in 1991. The Basilica of Saint-Remi is the largest Romanesque church in northern France. The city lies on the northern edge of the Champagne wine region, and many of the major champagne houses have their headquarters there.
rembrandt: Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was born on 15 July 1606 in Leiden, in the Dutch Republic, the ninth child of Harmen Gerritszoon van Rijn and Neeltgen Willemsdochter van Zuijtbrouck. The family was quite well-to-do: his father was a miller and his mother a baker's daughter. His mother was Catholic and his father belonged to the Dutch Reformed Church. As a boy he attended a Latin school and in 1620 enrolled at Leiden University, but he leaned towards painting and was soon apprenticed to Jacob van Swanenburg, with whom he spent three years. He then spent six months with the history painter Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam, and a few months with Jacob Pynas in 1625.

In 1625 Rembrandt opened a studio in Leiden, which he shared with his friend and colleague Jan Lievens. He began to accept students in 1627, among them Gerrit Dou and Isaac de Jouderville. In 1629 the statesman Constantijn Huygens discovered him and procured important commissions from the court at The Hague, and Prince Frederik Hendrik went on buying his paintings.

At the end of 1631 he moved to Amsterdam, a city rapidly expanding as a centre of business and trade, and practised as a professional portraitist for the first time, with great success. He first stayed with the art dealer Hendrick van Uylenburgh and in 1634 married Hendrick's cousin Saskia van Uylenburgh. That year he became a citizen of Amsterdam and a member of the local painters' guild. He ran a large workshop, and his pupils included Ferdinand Bol and Govert Flinck. His influence on painters around him was so great that it is hard to tell who worked in his studio and who only copied his style.

Unlike most Dutch painters of the 17th century, Rembrandt worked in a wide range of styles and subjects: portraits and self-portraits, landscapes, genre scenes, allegorical and historical scenes, biblical and mythological subjects and animal studies. He never went abroad, but was influenced by the Italian Old Masters and by Dutch and Flemish artists who had studied in Italy. His roughly 100 self-portraits, over 40 of them paintings, form an intimate autobiography. Among his best-known works are The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp (1632) and The Night Watch (1642). In 1633 he began signing with the spelling Rembrandt, adding a d to the Rembrant he had used before.

The size of his surviving output has been revised. Early in the 20th century connoisseurs credited him with well over 600 paintings, nearly 400 etchings and 2,000 drawings. The Rembrandt Research Project, begun in 1968, reassessed the attributions with technical methods, and recent scholarship puts his paintings nearer 300. His prints number slightly under 300.
renaissance: Many scholars place the origin of the Renaissance in Florence at the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries, with the writings of Dante Alighieri and Petrarch and the paintings of Giotto di Bondone. One proposed starting point is 1401, when Lorenzo Ghiberti and Filippo Brunelleschi competed for the contract for the bronze doors of the Baptistery of Florence Cathedral. Italy was divided into city-states and was one of the most urbanised areas of Europe, with many cities standing among Roman ruins.

Scholars have pointed to the Black Death of 1348 to 1350 and to the patronage of the Medici banking family, but no single factor fully explains why it began in Florence. Historians disagree on whether the Renaissance broke with the Middle Ages or extended them.

Renaissance humanism was less a philosophy than a method of learning. Humanists studied ancient texts in their original languages and appraised them with reasoning and empirical evidence, rather than resolving contradictions between authors as medieval scholastics did. Their education rested on the Studia Humanitatis: poetry, grammar, history, moral philosophy and rhetoric. In the 14th century scholars such as Petrarch and Poggio Bracciolini searched European libraries for Latin works by authors such as Cicero, Lucretius, Livy and Seneca. By the early 15th century a Greek phase was under way, recovering Greek literary, historical and theological texts.

In art, the Renaissance developed linear perspective. Giotto is credited with first treating a painting as a window into space, and Brunelleschi and Leon Battista Alberti formalised the technique. Printing with movable type, from a single shop in Mainz around 1440, had spread to around 270 cities and produced more than 20 million volumes by the end of the 15th century. Navigation also advanced: Columbus sailed in 1492 and the Magellan–Elcano expedition made the first circumnavigation between 1519 and 1522.

From Florence the Renaissance spread across Italy and by the 16th century through Europe, changing as it met local cultures. Albrecht Dürer and the printing press marked its arrival in Germany, Erasmus was the best-known humanist of the Netherlands, and the Elizabethan era is usually seen as the height of the English Renaissance. Many leading theologians, including Erasmus, Huldrych Zwingli, Thomas More, Martin Luther and John Calvin, followed the humanist method.

The artist and writer Giorgio Vasari first used the term rinascita in The Lives of the Artists (1550). The word Renaissance comes from French and was popularised by the historian Jules Michelet in 1855. The term has also been applied to earlier revivals, such as the Carolingian and Ottonian Renaissances and the Renaissance of the 12th century.
rene-descartes: René Descartes was born in La Haye en Touraine, in the Province of Touraine, on 31 March 1596. His mother, Jeanne Brochard, died in May 1597, a few days after giving birth to a stillborn child, and he lived with his grandmother and great-uncle. His father, Joachim, was a member of the Parlement of Rennes. In 1607, late because of his fragile health, he entered the Jesuit College of La Flèche, where he was introduced to mathematics and physics. He then studied at the University of Poitiers and took a degree in canon and civil law in 1616, as his father wished.

His Discourse on the Method of 1637 introduced essays on optics, meteorology and geometry. The Meditations on First Philosophy followed in 1641, and the Principles of Philosophy, a Latin textbook meant to replace the Aristotelian ones used in universities, in 1644. The Discourse appeared in a single edition of 500 copies, and the French edition of the Meditations had not sold out by his death, but a Latin edition of the Meditations was a commercial success. He died on 11 February 1650.

Descartes used hyperbolic doubt: he rejected any idea that could be doubted, then tried to rebuild knowledge on a firm foundation. The first principle he reached was that he thinks, expressed as cogito, ergo sum, or I think, therefore I am. Since doubting needs a doubter, the fact of doubt proved his existence. He concluded that perceiving his body through the senses was unreliable evidence, and that the only indubitable knowledge was that he is a thinking thing.

In mathematics he and Pierre de Fermat developed analytic geometry, which uses algebra to describe geometry; the Cartesian coordinate system is named after him. He is credited with representing unknowns by x, y and z and with using superscripts for powers. In his Principles he stated three laws of motion and claimed that the total quantity of motion in the universe is conserved, and Isaac Newton's laws were later modelled on his exposition. By shifting the question from what is true to what he could be certain of, he is often called the father of modern Western philosophy.
rennes: Rennes lies in the east of Brittany, in northwestern France, at the confluence of the rivers Ille and Vilaine. The ancient centre is built on a hill, with the north side higher than the south. The city is about 50 km from the English Channel, near Saint-Malo, Dinard and Mont Saint-Michel, and has an oceanic climate with much less rain than western Brittany. A protected green belt lies between the dense city and the rural parts of its urban area.

Rennes goes back more than 2,000 years, to a small Gallic village named Condate. Together with Vannes and Nantes it was one of the major cities of the old Duchy of Brittany. From the early 16th century until the French Revolution it was the parliamentary, administrative and garrison city of the province of Brittany within the Kingdom of France, as its 17th-century Parlement de Bretagne shows. The city played an important role in the Stamped Paper Revolt of 1675.

Its ramparts were built between the 3rd and the 12th centuries and were largely destroyed between the early 16th century and the 1860s. In 1720 a great fire destroyed most of the timber-framed houses in the northern part of the city. The north was rebuilt in stone on a grid plan, while the poorer southern part was not. Because the Parlement sat there, many hôtels particuliers were built in the richer northern half in the 18th century.

Rennes remained mostly rural until the Second World War. From the 1950s it grew through migration from the countryside and modern industry, partly in the automotive sector, and in the 1980s it became a centre of telecommunications and high-tech industry.

Rennes is the prefecture of the Brittany region and of the Ille-et-Vilaine department, with 230,890 inhabitants in 2023. It is labelled a city of art and history, with over 90 buildings protected as historic monuments. The Parlement de Bretagne, its main 17th-century building, was rebuilt after a fire in 1994 and houses the Rennes Court of Appeal. Colourful half-timbered houses survive along streets such as Saint-Georges and Saint-Michel, and the weekly Marché des Lices is one of the largest markets in France.
republic-of-serbian-krajina: The name Krajina, meaning frontier, came from the Military Frontier that the Habsburg monarchy carved out of Croatia and Slavonia between 1553 and 1578 against the Ottoman Empire. In the 1991 census Serbs made up about 12.2 per cent of the population of Croatia. After Franjo Tuđman was elected president of Croatia in April 1990, the Serb Democratic Party of Jovan Rašković broke with the Croatian parliament. In August 1990 Serbs blocked roads with logs in what became known as the Log Revolution, cutting Dalmatia off from the rest of the country, and a referendum confined to Serbs backed Serb sovereignty and autonomy by 99.7 per cent.

The Croatian constitution of December 1990 reduced the Serbs from a constituent people to a national minority. On 21 December 1990 the administration of Milan Babić announced a Serbian Autonomous Oblast of Krajina, which on 1 April 1991 declared that it would secede from Croatia.

Wider war began in August 1991. Between August and December approximately 80,000 Croats were expelled and some were killed; estimates of all exiled Croats and other non-Serbs range from 170,000, the figure of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, to a quarter of a million, that of Human Rights Watch. On 19 December 1991 the autonomous oblasts of Krajina and Western Slavonia proclaimed the republic, and that of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Syrmia was added on 26 February 1992.

The Vance plan and the Sarajevo Agreement of January 1992 established four United Nations Protected Areas and froze the front lines for three years. Refugees were not allowed to return. Babić, who opposed the plan, was replaced as president on 26 February 1992 by Goran Hadžić; Milan Martić won the presidency in January 1994. The economy depended wholly on the rump Yugoslavia: by 1994 only 36,000 of 430,000 citizens were employed. Croatian forces took Western Slavonia in Operation Flash in May 1995.

In Operation Storm between 150,000 and 200,000 Serbs fled, and only 5,000 to 6,000, mostly elderly, remained; some who refused to leave were murdered, tortured or expelled by the Croatian army and police. The remaining territory in eastern Slavonia was placed under a United Nations transitional authority by the Erdut Agreement and returned to Croatia in 1998.

The tribunal sentenced Babić, who pleaded guilty, to 13 years in 2004 and Milan Martić to 35 years in 2007. The Croatian generals Ante Gotovina and Mladen Markač were convicted in April 2011 of crimes during Operation Storm and acquitted on appeal in November 2012.
republic-of-the-congo: The Republic of the Congo lies on the western coast of Central Africa, west of the Congo River, along the Equator. It is bounded by Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Angolan exclave of Cabinda, and has 170 kilometres of beaches on the Atlantic. The southwest is a coastal plain drained by the Kouilou-Niari River, and the interior is a central plateau between two basins. The climate is consistent year-round, with a dry season from June to August.

The country is named after the Congo River, whose name derives from Kongo, a Bantu kingdom at its mouth around the time the Portuguese first arrived in 1483 or 1484. It is a distinct country from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its capital, Brazzaville, is named for the colony's founder, Pierre Savorgnan de Brazzà. Under France it was known as the French Congo or Middle Congo.

Bantu-speaking peoples mostly displaced and absorbed the earlier inhabitants, the Pygmy peoples, about 1500 BCE. By the 13th century there were three main federations of states in the western Congo Basin: the Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza in the east, Mpemba to its south, and a confederation of Vungu, Kakongo and Ngoyo to the west across the Congo River. The Tio Kingdom formed in the 14th century. The association of kingship with smithing is believed to have originated among the Tio before spreading to Loango and Kongo.

The Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo in 1484, and trade grew between the inland kingdoms and European merchants, who dealt in commodities, manufactured goods and enslaved people. The area north of the river came under French sovereignty in 1880 through Pierre de Brazza's treaty with the Tio king Iloo I, and Iloo's widow, Queen Ngalifourou, upheld its terms. In 1908 France organised French Equatorial Africa, with Brazzaville as federal capital. The Congo–Ocean Railway, built after the First World War, has been estimated to have cost at least 14,000 lives.

The Republic of the Congo became independent from France in 1960 and was a Marxist–Leninist state under the name People's Republic of the Congo from 1969 into the early 1990s. Its capital is Brazzaville. French is the official language, with Kituba and Lingala as national languages, and the Kongo are the largest ethnic group, roughly half of the population. Most of the population lives in the southwest, in Brazzaville, Pointe-Noire and the towns along the railway that joins them.
republican-party-united-states: The Republican Party began in 1854 as an anti-slavery party, formed to oppose the expansion of slavery into the western territories after the Democrats under Stephan Douglas passed the Kansas-Nebraska Act. It was formed in the Northern and Border states but not in the South, and it rapidly gained support in the North, drawing in former Whigs, Free Soil Democrats and former Know Nothings. It emerged as the main rival of the Democratic Party, and the two have dominated American politics since.

The founders chose the name in homage to the republican values of the Democratic-Republican Party that Thomas Jefferson had called the Republican Party. The idea came from an editorial by the party's leading publicist, Horace Greeley, who asked for a simple name like Republican to designate those who had united to restore the Union to its true mission as champion of liberty.

Abraham Lincoln's election as president in 1860 led to the secession of Southern states and the outbreak of the American Civil War. Under Lincoln and a Republican-controlled Congress the party led the effort to preserve the Union, defeat the Confederacy and abolish slavery. By 1865 it encompassed northern Protestants, factory workers, professionals, businessmen, prosperous farmers and black former slaves. Radical Republicans, hard-line abolitionists, pressed for abolition as a war aim and clashed with Lincoln's moderate Reconstruction plans. During Reconstruction the party sought to extend civil rights protections to freedmen, and by the late 1870s it turned its attention to business interests and industrial expansion.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it dominated national politics, promoting protective tariffs and infrastructure development. In the 20th century it split between an Old Right and a moderate faction in the Northeast, and opposition to Roosevelt's New Deal produced the conservative coalition. After the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the Southern states became more reliably Republican in presidential elections. The party won five of the six presidential elections from 1968 to 1988, and Ronald Reagan, in office from 1981 to 1989, was a transformative leader.

The nickname Grand Old Party originated in 1875 in the Congressional Record, which referred to the party of the Union's military defence as this gallant old party. The following year the Cincinnati Commercial used the phrase grand old party, and the abbreviation GOP is first recorded in 1884. Nineteen Republicans have served as president, the most from any single party.
rhine: The Rhine is about 1,230 kilometres long and drains an area of 185,000 square kilometres. It begins in the Swiss canton of Graubünden, where the Anterior Rhine, traditionally traced to Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass, joins the Posterior Rhine near Reichenau. As the Alpine Rhine it turns north near Chur and forms the Swiss border with Liechtenstein and Austria before entering Lake Constance.

The High Rhine runs west from Stein am Rhein over the Rhine Falls and is joined by the Aare, which more than doubles its discharge. At Basel the river bends north through the Upper Rhine Plain, takes in the Neckar, the Main and the Moselle, and from Bonn runs through the North German Plain as the Lower Rhine. In the Netherlands it forms, with the Meuse and the Scheldt, the largest river delta in Europe, splitting into the Waal, the Nederrijn and the IJssel.

About 11,000 years ago the Rhine's estuary lay in the Strait of Dover, and dry land called Doggerland still joined Britain to the continent until the sea overtopped it about 9,000 years ago. The river enters recorded history in the 1st century BCE, when Roman geographers made it the boundary between Gaul and Germania. By then La Tène culture covered almost its whole length, and the Upper Rhine formed a contact zone between Celtic and Germanic peoples. The Rhine and the Danube made up much of the Roman Empire's northern inland boundary.

By the 6th century the Rhine lay within Francia. In the 9th century it formed part of the border between Middle and Eastern Francia, and in the 10th century it lay wholly within the Holy Roman Empire. The mouths of the Rhine, in the county of Holland, passed to the Burgundian Netherlands in the 15th century. Archduke Sigismund of Austria sold Alsace to Burgundy in 1469, and it fell to France in the Thirty Years' War. When the Holy Roman Empire collapsed, the length of the river fell to the First French Empire and its client states. The many castles along the river show its importance as a trade route.

Among the largest cities on the Rhine are Cologne, Rotterdam, Düsseldorf, Duisburg, Strasbourg, Mannheim, Ludwigshafen, Arnhem and Basel. It passes through four countries and forms six different country borders. The German states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Rhineland-Palatinate and the French departments of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin take their names from it, and its name derives from the Gaulish Rēnos.
rhineland-palatinate: Rhineland-Palatinate is a landlocked state in western Germany, bordering France, Luxembourg and Belgium. Its major rivers are the Rhine, including the Middle Rhine, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Moselle. The northern half is formed by the Rhenish Massif, which includes the Eifel, the Moselle Valley, the Hunsrück and the Westerwald, while the Palatinate and Rhenish Hesse form most of the southern half. The mild climate of the deep Rhine and Moselle valleys allows fig, olive and almond trees to grow there. Forests cover 42 percent of the area.

The region has a long history, from the control of the Franks to the Holy Roman Empire, and saw fighting in both world wars. The league of ShUM cities, the Jewish communities of Mainz, Speyer and Worms, became the centre of Jewish life in medieval times. The state itself is young. The French military administration formed it on 30 August 1946, mainly from the southern part of the Prussian Rhine Province, Rhenish Hesse, the western part of Nassau and the Bavarian Rhenish Palatinate, and it was the last state in the Western Zone of Occupation to be established. The name Rhineland-Palatinate was first confirmed in the constitution adopted by referendum on 18 May 1947.

War damage meant that Mainz could not house the new administration, and the government and parliament sat provisionally in Koblenz until the Landtag decided on 16 May 1950 to move to Mainz. A sense of community developed only gradually in a state drawn up largely without regard to its inhabitants' historical affiliations. Referendums held on 19 January 1975 on transferring regions to other states produced no majority anywhere.

The state has about 4.05 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Mainz. It became part of the Federal Republic of Germany in 1949. Six of Germany's thirteen quality wine regions lie within it, Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Mosel, Nahe, Mittelrhein and Ahr, and between 65 and 70 percent of the country's wine grapes originate there. The chemical industry, represented by BASF at Ludwigshafen, is the principal employer.
rhodes: Rhodes is the largest of Greece's Dodecanese islands and their historical capital, and the ninth largest island in the Mediterranean. It lies northeast of Crete and southeast of Athens. The island is shaped like a spearhead, 79.7 kilometres long and 38 across at its widest, with an area of about 1,400 square kilometres. The city of Rhodes stands at the northern tip, at the site of the ancient and modern harbours. The interior is mountainous and forested with pine and cypress. Its Greek name, Ródos, resembles the word for rose, and it is called the Island of the Sun after its patron god Helios.

Humans lived on Rhodes from at least the late Neolithic. Urban settlements such as Asomatos arose at the end of the third millennium BCE, the Minoan Civilisation established a settlement at Tiranda in the sixteenth century BCE, and Mycenaean Greeks settled in the fifteenth. The Dorians who came in the eighth century BCE built the three cities of Lindus, Ialysus and Camirus. Athens defeated the Persians, who had overrun the island, in 478 BCE, and the Rhodian cities joined the Athenian League.

In the third century BCE the Rhodo-Egyptian alliance with the Ptolemies of Alexandria controlled trade through the Aegean. The Colossus of Rhodes, completed in 280 BCE, fell in an earthquake in 226 BCE. In 164 BCE Rhodes concluded a formal alliance with Rome, which confirmed Rome's predominance in the eastern Mediterranean.

The Byzantine period began in 395, and Rhodes became capital of the Roman province of the Islands. The Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem ruled the island from 1310 to 1522, and an earthquake on 3 May 1481 destroyed much of the city. Under the Ottomans the Kahal Shalom Synagogue was established in 1557. Italy seized Rhodes in 1912, and Turkey ceded it by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. German forces occupied it after the Italian Armistice of 8 September 1943, and most of the Jewish community was deported and killed. The island was ceded to Greece in 1947.

Rhodes forms a municipality of the South Aegean region, with 125,113 inhabitants in 2022. The medieval Old Town of the City of Rhodes is a World Heritage Site. The predominant religion is Greek Orthodox, with Latin Catholic, Muslim and Jewish communities as well. The Kahal Shalom Synagogue, in the Jewish quarter of the old town, is the oldest synagogue in Greece.
richard-i-of-england: Richard was born on 8 September 1157, probably at Beaumont Palace in Oxford, the third of five sons of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. As a younger son he was not expected to become king, but his two elder brothers died before their father. By the age of 16 he had taken command of his own army to put down rebellions in Poitou against his father. When Henry the Young King led a revolt against Henry II, Richard joined him at the French court, where Louis VII supported them and knighted Richard.

Richard was crowned in Westminster Abbey on 3 September 1189. A rumour that he had ordered all Jews killed set off an attack on the Jews of London, with homes burnt and some forcibly converted. Richard had taken the cross in 1187, and he and Philip II of France agreed to go on the Third Crusade together, each fearing that the other might usurp his lands in his absence.

In Sicily he captured Messina on 4 October 1190, and a treaty with Tancred was signed on 4 March 1191. He took Lemesos on Cyprus on 1 May 1191 after its ruler Isaac Komnenos refused to release prisoners and treasure, and married Berengaria of Navarre there on 12 May. He landed at Acre on 8 June 1191, supporting Guy of Lusignan against Conrad of Montferrat for the kingship of Jerusalem.

On the way home he was captured shortly before Christmas 1192 near Vienna by Leopold of Austria, who accused him of arranging the murder of Conrad of Montferrat. During his captivity his brother John revolted with Philip's help, and Philip took part of Normandy. Richard forgave John and named him his heir. He was crowned a second time at Winchester on 11 March 1194. He spent perhaps as little as six months of his reign in England.

In March 1199 Richard was in Limousin putting down a revolt and besieging the castle of Châlus-Chabrol. On 26 March he was struck in the shoulder by a crossbow bolt, and the wound turned gangrenous. He died on 6 April 1199. According to some accounts he forgave the crossbowman and had him freed with 100 shillings.

Contemporaries admired him as a king and knight famed for martial prowess, though some also called him cruel. Later historians sometimes judged that he treated England only as a source of revenue, a view that modern scholars regard as anachronistic given his continental responsibilities. His second Great Seal of 1198 is the first to show three lions passant-guardant, a design that later became the Royal Arms of England.
richard-nixon: Richard Milhous Nixon was born on 9 January 1913 in Yorba Linda, California, in a house his father built on the family's lemon ranch. His mother, Hannah Milhous Nixon, was a Quaker, and his father, Francis A. Nixon, converted from Methodism to the Quaker faith. Offered a tuition grant to attend Harvard University, he stayed at home because his brother Harold's illness needed his mother's care, and enrolled at Whittier College in September 1930.

He graduated from Whittier in 1934 and from Duke University School of Law in 1937, was admitted to the California bar that year and practised law in Whittier. In January 1942 he and his wife Pat moved to Washington, D.C., where he worked at the Office of Price Administration. Although he could have claimed an exemption as a birthright Quaker, he sought a commission and was appointed a lieutenant junior grade in the Naval Reserve on 15 June 1942.

Nixon won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1946, defeating Jerry Voorhis, and entered the Senate in 1950 after a bitter campaign against Helen Gahagan Douglas, in which opponents first called him Tricky Dick. As running mate of Dwight D. Eisenhower he served as vice president from 1953 to 1961. He lost the 1960 presidential election narrowly to John F. Kennedy and the 1962 race for governor of California to Pat Brown, then moved to New York. In 1968 he defeated Hubert Humphrey and was inaugurated on 20 January 1969.

His visit to China in 1972 led to diplomatic relations between the two nations, and his first term also saw the end of American combat involvement in Vietnam in 1973, the Apollo 11 Moon landing, the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency and the end of the dollar's direct convertibility to gold in 1971. He was re-elected in 1972, defeating George McGovern.

From 1973 revelations about the administration's part in Watergate, which began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee office ordered by administration officials, eroded his support in Congress and the country. On 9 August 1974, facing almost certain impeachment and removal, Nixon resigned, the only president to do so. On 8 September 1974 his successor, Gerald Ford, granted him a pardon. In nearly twenty years of retirement he wrote nine books and made many foreign trips, rehabilitating his image into that of an elder statesman. He suffered a stroke on 18 April 1994 and died four days later.
richard-wagner: Wilhelm Richard Wagner was born on 22 May 1813 in Leipzig into a family of musicians, the ninth and youngest child of Carl Friedrich Wagner, a clerk in the Leipzig police service, and Johanna Rosine Wagner, a baker's daughter. His father died of typhoid fever six months after his birth. His mother then lived with Carl's friend, the actor and playwright Ludwig Geyer, whom she probably married in August 1814, and the family moved to Dresden. Until he was fourteen Wagner was known as Wilhelm Richard Geyer, and he almost certainly believed Geyer to be his biological father.

Geyer's love of the theatre was shared by his stepson. At nine Wagner was greatly impressed by Carl Maria von Weber's opera Der Freischütz, which he saw Weber conduct. His first creative effort was a tragedy called Leubald, begun in 1826, and he persuaded his family to let him take music lessons. Back in Leipzig he studied harmony from 1828 to 1831. Hearing Beethoven's 7th and 9th symphonies in 1828 inspired him, and he wrote a piano transcription of the 9th.

Wagner wrote both the libretti, which he called poems, and the music of all his stage works. His earliest attempts at opera were often left unfinished. Rienzi (1842) was his first opera to be staged successfully, and he later said he did not consider his early works part of his oeuvre.

From 1849 he urged a new concept of opera, often called music drama, in which musical, poetic and dramatic elements were fused in a Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art. He set out these ideas in essays published between 1849 and 1852 and realised them most fully in the first half of The Ring of the Nibelung. The orchestra became as important as the singers, and leitmotifs, musical phrases tied to characters, places and plot elements, are interwoven through the drama. To stage his works he had the Bayreuth Festspielhaus built, which hosted the premieres of The Ring and Parsifal.

Wagner died on 13 February 1883. After his death his wife Cosima took over the leadership of the Bayreuth Festival, which has since remained under the management of their descendants. From Tristan und Isolde onwards he explored the limits of the traditional tonal system, and some music historians date the beginning of modern classical music to its first notes. Anton Bruckner, Hugo Wolf, Richard Strauss and Gustav Mahler were among the composers indebted to him.

He remained controversial in his lifetime and afterwards. His hostile writings on Jews, including Jewishness in Music, correspond to trends of thought in 19th-century Germany, though he also had Jewish friends and supporters. The extent to which antisemitic stereotypes appear in his operas is debated.
richmond-virginia: Richmond stands at the fall line of the James River, the rocky point that separates Virginia's Piedmont from the Tidewater and the highest point the river can be navigated. The Piedmont is a region of low, rolling hills lying between the flat Tidewater and the Blue Ridge Mountains. The site was an important village in the Powhatan Confederacy; the name of the Powhatan people is traced to Pawat-hanne, meaning falls in a stream, a reference to the falls of the James. After Jamestown was founded in April 1607, Captain Christopher Newport led explorers up the river to this inhabited area.

English colonists from Jamestown briefly settled the place from 1609 to 1611. Richmond was founded in 1737, with a street grid laid out between what are now Broad, 17th and 25th Streets and the river, and was incorporated in 1742.

In 1775 Patrick Henry delivered his speech ending 'Give me liberty or give me death!' at St. John's Church. The state capital moved there from Williamsburg on 18 April 1780, partly to give a more central position for Virginia's growing western population. In 1781 Loyalist troops led by Benedict Arnold raided and burned the city, and Governor Thomas Jefferson fled. Richmond recovered quickly. The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, drafted by Jefferson, was enacted in 1786, and the State Capitol, designed by Jefferson and Charles-Louis Clérisseau in the Greek Revival style, was completed in 1788.

The Virginia Convention voted to secede from the United States on 17 April 1861, five days after the attack on Fort Sumter, pending a popular vote. On 20 May the Confederate States Congress voted to move its capital from Montgomery, Alabama, to Richmond, and on 23 May Virginia voters ratified the Ordinance of Secession. After the war the city again became a major centre of production, with iron-front buildings and large brick factories, a railway crossroads with what is described as the world's first triple railway crossing, and a centre of tobacco processing.

Richmond is the capital of Virginia and has been an independent city since 1871; its population was 226,610 at the 2020 census. In the early twentieth century its Jackson Ward, a business district built by freed people and their descendants, was known as the Wall Street of Black America, and in 1903 Maggie L. Walker chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank and became the first Black woman to serve as a bank president in the United States. The city contains many buildings in Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival styles, among others, and has designated 45 historic districts.
rio-de-janeiro: Rio de Janeiro lies near the west end of a strip of Brazil's Atlantic coast, close to the Tropic of Capricorn, where the shoreline runs east and west, so the city faces largely south. It was founded at the entrance to an inlet, Guanabara Bay, which is marked by a point of land called Sugar Loaf. The city occupies 1,182.3 square kilometres, and its residents are known as cariocas. Its parks include the Tijuca National Park, a national park since 1961, and the Passeio Público, described as the first public park in the Americas.

The region was inhabited by the Tupi, Puri, Botocudo and Maxakalí peoples. Europeans first encountered Guanabara Bay on 1 January 1502 during a Portuguese expedition, which gave the bay and then the city its name, meaning January River. In 1555 some 500 French colonists under Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon occupied an island in the bay and built Fort Coligny, attempting to found the colony of France Antarctique. The Portuguese saw it as a threat, and from 1560 a long military campaign led by Governor General Mem de Sá and later his nephew Estácio de Sá ended on 20 January 1567 in the defeat and expulsion of the French.

Estácio de Sá founded the city proper on 1 March 1565 and named it São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro, after the patron saint of the Portuguese king Sebastião. Until early in the 18th century it was threatened or invaded by pirates and buccaneers, mostly French. In 1763 it became the capital of the State of Brazil, and in 1808 the Portuguese royal court moved there. Rio remained the capital of the Portuguese monarchy until 1822, the only instance in modern history in which the capital of a colonising country officially shifted to one of its colonies. It then served as capital of the Empire of Brazil until 1889, and of republican Brazil until 1960, when the capital moved to Brasília.

Rio de Janeiro is the capital of the state of Rio de Janeiro, with about 6 million people in the city proper. It is known for its carnival, samba and bossa nova, and for beaches such as Copacabana and Ipanema. Landmarks include the statue of Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado, Sugarloaf Mountain and the Maracanã Stadium.
rio-grande-do-norte: Rio Grande do Norte forms the north-eastern tip of the South American continent. Its name means Great Northern River and refers to the mouth of the Potengi river. The coast, about 410 kilometres of sandy beaches, dominates the state, and two climates meet there: humid tropical on the eastern coast and semi-arid over most of the rest, where much of the interior lies in the Polygon of Droughts. The state also includes Rocas Atoll, 260 kilometres north-east of Natal, the only atoll in the South Atlantic.

The first European to reach the region may have been the Spaniard Alonso de Ojeda in 1499. Cape São Roque, to the north of Natal, was visited in 1501 on the Portuguese expedition led by Amerigo Vespucci, which also named the Potengi river and the Rio Grande after which the captaincy and later the state were named. For decades no permanent European settlement was made among the Potiguara, who lived there, and between 1535 and 1598 French pirates came in search of brazilwood. The Portuguese built the Forte dos Reis Magos in 1598 and founded Natal the next year. Cattle and sugarcane then drove the local economy.

In 1633 the area became a battleground between the Portuguese and the Dutch. When sugar prices fell in Amsterdam, a crisis led settlers and native Brazilians to revolt against the Dutch, in what are known as the massacres of Cunhaú and Uruaçu. Religious conflict between Portuguese-Brazilian Catholicism and Dutch Calvinism, Portugal's restoration of its throne in 1640 and the reconquest of Maranhão in 1643 led to the uprising of 1645 under André Vidal de Negreiros and João Fernandes Vieira, in which most of the rebels were Africans and Amerindians. The Dutch were finally driven out in 1654. In the Second World War the state served as an Allied airbase, and in 1964 Latin America's first space launch site, Barreira do Inferno, was built there.

Natal is the capital and largest city, and the state has 167 municipalities and an estimated 3,568,765 inhabitants in 2021. Portuguese is the language of the state. The economy has relied on sugar and cattle, and now also on tourism, petroleum, fruit, sea salt, cashew and carnauba wax. The sixteenth-century Forte dos Reis Magos still stands, and the folklorist Luís da Câmara Cascudo was born and worked in the state.
rio-grande-do-sul: Rio Grande do Sul, meaning Great River of the South, lies in the southernmost part of Brazil. It is bordered by Santa Catarina to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the east, Uruguay to the south and southwest, and the Argentine provinces of Corrientes and Misiones to the west. Its climate is predominantly humid subtropical, and in winter a cold southwesterly wind called the minuano sometimes lowers the temperature below freezing.

Before the arrival of Portuguese and Spanish settlers the area was inhabited mostly by the Guarani and Kaingang peoples. The first Europeans there were Jesuits, followed by settlers from the Azores. By the Treaty of Tordesillas the region was to be Spanish, but Spain's interest lay on the Pacific coast and the River Plate, and the Spanish introduced livestock that escaped into the plains and attracted gauchos. The colonial province saw small wars and border skirmishes between Portugal and Spain. The Portuguese Crown distributed land in enormous latifundia, where cattle raising predominated, while Azorean settlers on smaller properties introduced wheat, the main export until the early 19th century.

In the 19th century the state was the scene of the Ragamuffin War, wars with Argentina and Uruguay, and the Paraguayan War. In the war against the Argentine dictator Juan Manuel Rosas, 75 percent of the Brazilian troops were gaúchos. In 1865 a Paraguayan division occupied Uruguaiana, and troops of the Triple Alliance besieged it until the Paraguayans surrendered. In 1930 Getúlio Vargas, then state president, led a revolt that overthrew the federal government.

Rio Grande do Sul is a state of Brazil divided into 497 municipalities, with Porto Alegre as its capital and largest city. It shares a gaucho culture with Argentina and Uruguay, and its people are known for drinking chimarrão, a local version of mate, and for eating churrasco. Large waves of German and Italian migration have shaped the state.
river-thames: The Thames rises at Thames Head in Gloucestershire, about 1.5 miles north of the village of Kemble in the Cotswolds, and flows into the North Sea near Tilbury in Essex and Gravesend in Kent via the Thames Estuary. It passes through Oxford, where it is sometimes called the Isis, and Reading, Henley-on-Thames and Windsor, and it drains the whole of Greater London. Its lower reaches, the Tideway, extend up to Teddington Lock. Along its course are 45 navigation locks, and the river contains over 80 islands.

Researchers have identified the Thames as a discrete drainage line as early as 58 million years ago. About 450,000 years ago, in the Anglian ice age, the ice sheet dammed the river in Hertfordshire, and the large ice lakes that formed eventually burst and diverted the river onto its present course through the area of London. The name derives from the Brittonic Tamesas, recorded in Latin as Tamesis.

Some of the earliest written references occur in Julius Caesar's account of his second expedition to Britain in 54 BCE, when the river presented a major obstacle and he met the Belgic tribes of the Catuvellauni and Atrebates along it. Until enough crossings existed the river was a formidable barrier, and Belgic tribes and Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were defined by which side of it they lay on. When English counties were established, their boundaries were partly set by the Thames.

In the early modern period the Stuart monarchs and the City of London organised pageants on the river. During cold winters it froze above London Bridge, and a tent city stood on it at the first Frost Fair in 1607. Four serious cholera outbreaks killed tens of thousands of people between 1832 and 1865, and in the Great Stink of 1858 sittings of the House of Commons had to be abandoned. A flood on 7 January 1928 drowned fourteen people in London, and together with the North Sea flood of 1953 helped lead to the Thames Barrier, built in the 1970s.

At 215 miles (346 km) the Thames is the longest river entirely in England and the second-longest in the United Kingdom, after the Severn. It is maintained for navigation by powered craft from the estuary as far as Lechlade, and it supplies drinking water, including through the Thames Water Ring Main in London. The river is the historic heartland of rowing in the United Kingdom. Handel's Water Music premiered on the river on 17 July 1717 for King George I.
riyadh: Riyadh is the largest city on the Arabian Peninsula. It lies in the eastern part of the Najd plateau, at an average elevation of 600 metres above sea level. The climate is hot desert, with long, extremely hot summers and short, cold winters. The city is known for dust storms so thick that visibility can fall under 10 m. The old town within the walls did not exceed an area of 1 km2, and the city is now divided into fourteen branch municipalities and the Diplomatic Quarter.

In the pre-Islamic era the city on the site was called Hajr and was reportedly founded by the tribe of Banu Hanifa. It was the capital of the province of Al-Yamama, whose governors were responsible for most of central and eastern Arabia under the Umayyad Caliphate and Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Yamama broke away from the Abbasid Caliphate in 866, and the Banu Ukhaidhir, who then ruled the area, moved the capital to nearby Al-Kharj. Hajr went into a long decline. In the 14th century Ibn Battuta visited it, and described it as the main city of Al-Yamama, a city of canals and trees whose inhabitants mostly belonged to the Banu Hanifa.

Hajr later broke up into separate settlements and estates, the most notable being Migrin and Mi'kal. The earliest known reference to the area as Riyadh, meaning gardens, comes from a 17th-century chronicler describing an event of 1590. Dahham ibn Dawwas, a refugee from neighbouring Manfuhah, took control and built a single wall around the various oasis towns, making them in effect one fortress city. Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the Emir of Diriyah, Muhammad bin Saud, then took the town from him, but the First Saudi state they formed collapsed in 1818. Turki ibn Abdullah founded the Second Saudi state in the early 19th century and made Riyadh his capital, though a joint Ottoman and Rashidi alliance disrupted his rule.

Ibn Saud retrieved his ancestral rule in 1902 with the Emirate of Riyadh and consolidated it by 1926 with the conquest of the Hejaz. In September 1932 he named his kingdom Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh as the capital. The first major construction beyond the walls was his Murabba Palace, built in 1936-1938, and the government moved there in 1938. In the 1950s the walls were dismantled and the modern city expanded from the old town. The population was 40,000 in 1935 and 83,000 in 1949. Of the old town the Al-Masmak Palace and parts of the wall and its gate survive, restored.
roald-amundsen: Roald Engelbregt Gravning Amundsen was born on 16 July 1872 in Borge, Østfold, into a family of Norwegian shipowners and captains. His mother wanted him to avoid the maritime trade and become a doctor, a promise he kept until she died when he was 21, after which he quit university for a life at sea. At fifteen he had been enthralled by Sir John Franklin's narratives of his Arctic expeditions. In 1897 he joined the Belgian Antarctic Expedition of Adrien de Gerlache as first mate; its ship Belgica became locked in sea ice and the first expedition to overwinter in Antarctica endured a winter for which it was poorly prepared.

In 1903 Amundsen led the first expedition to traverse the Northwest Passage, in the 45-ton sloop Gjøa with a crew of six. They spent two winters at King William Island, where the Netsilik Inuit taught them Arctic survival skills, such as using sled dogs and wearing animal skins instead of woolen parkas. The ship cleared the Canadian Arctic Archipelago on 17 August 1905, and the crew returned to Oslo in November 1906.

In 1909, hearing of the claims of Frederick Cook and Robert Peary to the North Pole, Amundsen turned to Antarctica without making clear his intentions, and Robert F. Scott felt misled. He left Oslo in the Fram on 3 June 1910 and set up base at Framheim in January 1911. Five men, Amundsen, Olav Bjaaland, Helmer Hanssen, Sverre Hassel and Oscar Wisting, left on 19 October with four sledges and 52 dogs and reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, a month before Scott's group. His success rested on careful preparation, skis, dogs and Inuit-style furred clothing.

From 1918 to 1925 Amundsen led an expedition in the ship Maud through the Northeast Passage, aiming to drift towards the North Pole as Fridtjof Nansen had; the ship froze in the ice and the goal was not achieved. On 12 May 1926 he and 15 other men in the airship Norge became the first explorers verified to have reached the North Pole. In June 1928 he disappeared while flying on a rescue mission for the airship Italia in the Arctic. The search for his remains, which have not been found, was called off that September.
robert-boyle: Robert Boyle was born at Lismore Castle in County Waterford on 25 January 1627, the seventh son and fourteenth child of Richard Boyle, 1st Earl of Cork, and Catherine Fenton. After his mother's death, when he was eight, he and his brother Francis were sent to Eton College. He then travelled abroad with a French tutor and spent the winter of 1641 in Florence, studying the paradoxes of the elderly Galileo Galilei. He returned to England in 1644, a year after his father's death, and lived at the manor of Stalbridge in Dorset until 1652, working in a laboratory and joining the band of enquirers known as the Invisible College.

Boyle moved to Ireland in 1652 but, frustrated in his chemical work, went to Oxford in 1654. Having read in 1657 of Otto von Guericke's vacuum pump, he set about improving it with Robert Hooke, and his Pneumatical Engine was finished in 1659. In answering the Jesuit Francis Line's objections to his account of the experiments he first mentioned the law that the volume of a gas varies inversely to its pressure. In continental Europe it is sometimes attributed to Edme Mariotte.

In 1663 the Invisible College became the Royal Society of London, and Charles II's charter named Boyle to its council. In 1680 he was elected president but declined from a scruple about oaths. From 1668 he lived in London in the house of his sister Katherine Jones, Lady Ranelagh, with whom he kept a lifelong intellectual partnership. He died on 31 December 1691, a week after her, and was buried at St Martin-in-the-Fields.

Boyle held that knowledge should rest on experiment, writing that he did not love to believe anything upon conjectures when a not over-difficult experiment could test it. He was also an alchemist who thought the transmutation of metals possible. In The Sceptical Chymist he criticised the Spagyrists who held that salt, sulphur and mercury were the true principles of things. He took elements to be the undecomposable constituents of bodies, distinguished mixtures from compounds and gave the name analysis to the detection of their ingredients.

A devout Anglican, he refused holy orders on the ground that his religious writings would carry more weight from a layman, and he argued that the design visible in nature showed God's involvement with the world. From 1680 to 1685 he paid for the printing of the Bible in Irish.
robert-louis-stevenson: Stevenson was born at 8 Howard Place, Edinburgh, on 13 November 1850 and christened Robert Lewis Balfour Stevenson.
