His father, Thomas Stevenson, was a leading lighthouse engineer, and lighthouse design was the family's profession. About the age of 18 he changed the spelling of Lewis to Louis. Serious bronchial trouble kept him from school for long periods. In November 1867 he entered the University of Edinburgh to study engineering but showed no enthusiasm, and in April 1871 he told his father he would pursue a life of letters. It was agreed that he should read law instead.

In late 1873 he met Sidney Colvin, who became his literary adviser. In 1876 he met Fanny Van de Grift Osbourne, an American and a magazine short-story writer, at Grez-sur-Loing. In 1884 the couple settled in Bournemouth. He is best known for Treasure Island (1883), Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Kidnapped (1886) and A Child's Garden of Verses (1885). W. E. Henley may have provided the model for Long John Silver.

In June 1888 he chartered the yacht Casco and sailed with his family from San Francisco. For nearly three years he wandered the eastern and central Pacific, staying in the Hawaiian Islands, where he befriended King Kalākaua, and visiting the Gilbert Islands, where he spent months on Abemama with the chief Tem Binoka, whom he described in In the South Seas. In December 1889 the family arrived at Apia in Samoa and decided to settle, buying land at Vailima in January 1890. Alarmed at growing European and American influence in the islands, he turned from romance toward realism, notably in The Beach of Falesá.

On 3 December 1894, at Vailima, Stevenson collapsed while talking to his wife and died within a few hours at the age of 44, possibly of a brain haemorrhage. He was a celebrity in his lifetime, admired by writers including Henry James and Rudyard Kipling, and half his original manuscripts, among them that of Treasure Island, are lost.
robert-mugabe: Robert Gabriel Mugabe was born on 21 February 1924 at the Kutama Mission village in Southern Rhodesia. His father was a carpenter and his mother a Christian catechist for the village children, and the family belonged to the Zezuru clan, one of the smallest branches of the Shona people. He worked as a schoolteacher, and in 1949 won a scholarship to the University of Fort Hare in South Africa. There he joined the youth league of the African National Congress and met Jewish South African communists who introduced him to Marxist ideas, though he later said his biggest influence was Mahatma Gandhi. He left in 1952 with a degree in history and English literature.

Mugabe returned to Southern Rhodesia in May 1960. He was arrested in December 1963 and sentenced in March 1964 for subversive statements. He remained in prison for eight years in Salisbury, studying and gaining several degrees from the University of London. In March 1975 he left for Mozambique, where President Samora Machel at first doubted his leadership and kept him under partial house arrest for almost a year before accepting him as head of ZANU. After the Lancaster House Agreement he returned to Salisbury in January 1980 and campaigned without Marxist or revolutionary rhetoric, as Machel had advised. ZANU-PF won the election.

Zimbabwe gained internationally recognised independence on 18 April 1980, and Mugabe took the oath as prime minister. He pledged racial reconciliation and invited members of rival parties into his cabinet. Relations with Joshua Nkomo's ZAPU deteriorated, and in the Gukurahundi of 1982 to 1987 the 5th Brigade crushed ZAPU-linked opposition in Matabeleland in a campaign that killed at least 20,000 people. On 30 December 1987 parliament made him executive president, with power to dissolve parliament and run for an unlimited number of terms.

From 2000 he encouraged black Zimbabweans to seize white-owned farms, and food production fell, followed by famine and hyperinflation. On 6 November 2017 he dismissed Vice-President Emmerson Mnangagwa, and on 15 November the army placed him under house arrest. He resigned, and Mnangagwa succeeded him. Mugabe died in Singapore on 6 September 2019.
robert-schumann: Robert Schumann was born on 8 June 1810 in Zwickau, in the Kingdom of Saxony, the fifth and last child of August Schumann and his wife Johanna Christiane. His father was a bookseller, lexicographer, author and publisher who made considerable sums from German translations of Cervantes, Walter Scott and Lord Byron, and Robert, his favourite child, spent many hours exploring the classics in his father's collection. August died in 1826, and Schumann's mother, less enthusiastic about a musical career, persuaded him to study law. He entered Leipzig University in 1828, but reading and playing the piano occupied much of his time. He discovered the works of Franz Schubert, whose death in November 1828 made him cry all night.

Schumann published his Op. 1, piano variations on a theme spelled from the name of Countess Pauline von Abegg, who was almost certainly his own invention. The use of a musical cryptogram became a recurrent feature of his later music. In 1832 he published Papillons, a programmatic piano piece. He came to regard himself as having two sides to his personality and art, and named his introspective self Eusebius and his impetuous alter ego Florestan. In 1840 he turned to song, producing more than half his total output of Lieder, including Myrthen, a wedding present for Clara, Frauenliebe und Leben and Dichterliebe.

In 1841 he focused on orchestral music. His First Symphony, The Spring, was premiered by Mendelssohn at the Gewandhaus on 31 March, at a concert where Clara also played. In 1842 he wrote three string quartets, a Piano Quintet, written for Clara, and a Piano Quartet. His opera Genoveva, premiered in Leipzig in June 1850, was not the success he hoped for, and Franz Liszt revived it at Weimar in 1855, the only other production in Schumann's lifetime. Schumann wrote more than 300 songs for voice and piano, favouring such later Romantic poets as Heine, Eichendorff and Mörike.

Schumann moved to Düsseldorf in 1850 as the city's director of music but resigned after three years, since his shyness and mental instability made it hard to work with his orchestra. In 1853 he met the twenty-year-old Johannes Brahms and praised him in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. The following year his mental health deteriorated gravely. He threw himself into the Rhine, was rescued and was taken to a private sanatorium near Bonn, where he died on 29 July 1856.

His reputation rests chiefly on the piano works and songs of the 1830s and 1840s. Later composers drew on him, among them Mahler, Richard Strauss, Arnold Schoenberg, Bizet, Fauré, Debussy and Ravel. Elgar called him his ideal, and Tchaikovsky, though critical of his orchestration, described him as a composer of genius.
roman-empire: By 100 BCE the city of Rome had expanded its rule from the Italian peninsula to most of the Mediterranean, but civil wars severely destabilised the Republic. They culminated in the victory of Octavian over Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE the Roman Senate granted Octavian overarching military power (imperium) and the title of Augustus, marking his accession as the first Roman emperor. The first two centuries of the Empire saw stability and prosperity known as the Pax Romana, and Rome reached its widest extent under Trajan (r. 98 to 117 CE).

Decline began under Commodus (r. 180 to 192). In the 3rd century a 50-year crisis of civil war, plagues and invasions threatened the Empire; the Gallic and Palmyrene empires broke away, and the Empire was reunified under Aurelian (r. 270 to 275). Diocletian (r. 284 to 305) set up two imperial courts, in the Greek East and the Latin West, and Constantine (r. 306 to 337), the first Christian emperor, moved the imperial seat to Byzantium in 330 and renamed it Constantinople. The Western Empire collapsed in 476, when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustus. The Eastern Empire survived until the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Provinces were either senatorial, governed by proconsuls appointed by lot each year, or imperial, belonging to the emperor and governed by legates. The Romans lacked the manpower to rule by force alone, so they cooperated with local elites, and communities that showed loyalty kept their own laws and could collect their own taxes. Latin and Greek were the main languages, and the Empire was deliberately multilingual. By the time of Nero it was not unusual to find a former slave richer than a freeborn citizen. Roman religion rested on correct ritual and sacrifice rather than faith or dogma, and as many as 135 days of the calendar were given to festivals and games.

Several states claimed to be the Empire's successor. The Holy Roman Empire was established in 800 when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Roman emperor, and the Russian Tsardom counted itself the Third Rome, Constantinople having been the second. When the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II made it his capital and claimed to sit on the throne of the Roman Empire. Rome's republican institutions influenced the Italian city-state republics, the early United States and modern democratic republics.
roman-republic: Rome had been ruled by monarchs elected for life by the Senate. Traditional histories say the last, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled in 509 BCE after his son Sextus Tarquinius raped a noblewoman, Lucretia, and that a revolution led by the semi-mythical Lucius Junius Brutus transferred the king's powers to two consuls elected for one year, each able to veto his colleague. Most modern scholarship describes these accounts as the quasi-mythological detailing of an aristocratic coup within Tarquin's own family, or a consequence of an Etruscan occupation of Rome, rather than a popular revolution.

Republican Rome was in a state of near-perpetual war. After the Gallic sack of Rome it conquered most of the Italian peninsula in a century. It fought three wars against Carthage and defeated it at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, then defeated Philip V and Perseus of Macedon, Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire and Vercingetorix of the Arverni. At home the plebs achieved political equality with the patricians by the 4th century BCE, ending the Conflict of the Orders peacefully.

From 133 BCE the late Republic saw substantial domestic strife. The Social War between Rome and its Italian allies over citizenship expanded civil violence, and mass slavery contributed to three Servile Wars. Powerful semi-autonomous generals led to civil wars, first between Marius and Sulla and in 49 BCE between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Erich S. Gruen holds that civil war caused the fall of the republic, not the reverse. It ended in 27 BCE with the establishment of the Roman Empire.

The constitution was an unwritten, evolving set of principles passed down through precedent. There were annual elections, but the system was an elective oligarchy, with powerful families largely monopolising the senior magistracies. The Senate's decrees were officially advice, yet magistrates usually followed them, and it came to control finances and external affairs. Consuls and praetors held imperium, the authority to command an army. Census figures report 130,000 Romans in 509 BCE and 4,937,000 in 14 CE. From 107 BCE all citizens, whatever their wealth, could enter the army, which became paid and attracted the poorest.
romani-people: Linguistic and genetic evidence suggests that the Romani originated in north-western regions of the Indian subcontinent, particularly in present-day Punjab, Rajasthan and Sindh. Because the Romani did not chronicle their history, most hypotheses about early Roma rest on linguistic data. Genetic findings published in 2012 suggest that the ancestors of present-day scheduled caste and scheduled tribe populations of northern India, traditionally called the Doma, are the likely ancestral populations of European Roma.

Historians now believe the westward migration, possibly in waves, occurred around 1000 CE, perhaps in the context of the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni. The Romani moved west into the Ghaznavid Empire and later the Byzantine Empire. Armenian-origin words in Romani indicate that they passed through Armenia.

The Romani arrived in Europe through the Balkans, probably in the twelfth century. A document of 1068 from Constantinople mentions Atsingani, probably meaning Roma. The English word Gypsy comes from Egipcien, the medieval belief that they were itinerant Egyptians. Their reception was mixed. The first recorded transaction for a Romani slave in Wallachia dates to 1385, while Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund issued them safe conduct in 1417.

Expulsions followed: from the Meissen region of Germany in 1416, Lucerne in 1471, Milan in 1493, France in 1504, Catalonia in 1512, Sweden in 1525, England in 1530 and Denmark in 1536. From 1510 any Roma found in Switzerland were to be executed, and Portugal began deporting Roma to its colonies in 1538. Large-scale emigration to the Americas began in the 1860s. In the mid- to late twentieth century forced sterilisation in several European countries reduced Roma populations.

The Romani traditionally led a nomadic, itinerant life. Many subgroups and clans name themselves, among them the Sinti, Kalderash, Lovari and Manouche. The Romani language is Indo-Aryan with strong Persian, Armenian, Greek and South Slavic influence, and its dialects have more than 2 million speakers. Romanipen is the totality of the Romani spirit, culture, law and identity. The first World Romani Congress in 1971 voted to reject all exonyms for the Romani, including Gypsy.
romania: Romania lies on the lower course of the Danube and on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea. It covers 238,397 square kilometres, and its terrain is distributed roughly equally between mountains, hills and plains. The Carpathian Mountains dominate the centre, with 14 ranges reaching above 2,000 metres; the highest is Moldoveanu Peak at 2,544 metres. They are surrounded by the Moldavian and Transylvanian plateaus, the Pannonian Plain and the Wallachian plains.

The Danube flows into the Black Sea and forms the Danube Delta, the second-largest and best-preserved delta in Europe. At 5,800 square kilometres it is the largest continuous marshland in Europe. Romania has one of the largest areas of undisturbed forest in Europe, covering almost 27% of its territory, and about 50% of Europe's brown bears outside Russia.

Human remains from Peștera cu Oase, about 40,000 years old, are the oldest known Homo sapiens in Europe. Salt production at the Poiana Slatinei site began between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE, the earliest evidence for salt exploitation in Europe, and the Cucuteni-Trypillia culture flourished in the 3rd millennium BCE. Greek colonies were established on the Black Sea coast in the 7th century BCE. Burebista, the first Dacian ruler to unite the local tribes, conquered the Greek colonies in Dobruja between around 55 and 44 BCE, and his kingdom collapsed after he was murdered in 44 BCE.

Part of the territory became the Roman province of Dacia after Trajan's Dacian Wars. The modern state was formed in 1859 through the union of Moldavia and Wallachia under Alexandru Ioan Cuza and took the name Romania in 1866. The Great Union of 1918 and the treaties that followed created Greater Romania, which reached its largest territorial extent. King Michael I was forced to abdicate in December 1947, and the communist Romanian People's Republic followed. The revolution of 1989 ended communism.

Romania is a semi-presidential republic with a bicameral Parliament of a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies. It joined the European Union in 2007 and is a member of NATO. The 2021 census counted 19,053,815 people, of whom 89.33% were Romanians, 6.05% Hungarians and 3.44% Roma; the Council of Europe puts the Roma figure higher, at 8.32%.

The name derives from the endonym român, from Latin romanus. The oldest surviving document in Romanian is Neacșu's letter, which mentions Țeara Rumânească, the Romanian Land, meaning Wallachia. About 12 million Romanians and people with Romanian-born ancestors live abroad.
romanticism: Romanticism originated in Europe towards the end of the 18th century, in response to the Age of Enlightenment and the Industrial Revolution. Its first ideas arose from an earlier German Counter-Enlightenment movement, Sturm und Drang (Storm and Stress), which criticised the Enlightenment claim that humans can fully comprehend the world through reason alone. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's The Sorrows of Young Werther, published in 1774, helped to shape its ideals.

The period varies by country and art. Scholars of English literature place it between about 1789 or 1798 and about 1830, and the publication of Lyrical Ballads by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1798 is often held to mark its start. The consensus is that it peaked between 1800 and 1850.

Romantics rejected the social conventions of their time in favour of individualism, and argued that passion and intuition were crucial to understanding the world. Beauty, they held, was more than form, since it evokes a strong emotional response. Their recurring themes were a reverence for nature and the supernatural, an idealisation of the past as a nobler era, a fascination with the exotic and mysterious, and a celebration of the heroic and the sublime.

They preferred the medieval to the classical, seeing the Middle Ages as an age of chivalry and a more organic relationship between humans and their surroundings, in contrast to an industrial society they thought alienating. The movement shaped literature, painting, music and architecture, and touched politics: Romantic thinking influenced conservatism, liberalism, radicalism and nationalism. In Poland it is often taken to begin with Adam Mickiewicz's first poems in 1822 and to end with the suppression of the January Uprising of 1863 against the Russians, and was strongly marked by interest in Polish history.

By the First World War the cultural climate had changed so far that Romanticism had dispersed into later movements. Late Romantic figures such as Rachmaninoff, who died in the 1940s, were widely respected but seen as anachronisms. Romantic nationalism has been judged to have had a largely negative effect on 19th-century history writing, because each nation tended to produce its own version of the past with clear heroes and villains.

Romantic thought and art went on to influence art and music, speculative fiction, philosophy, politics and environmentalism. The modern sense of romanticising something often has little to do with the historical movement.
rome: Rome lies in the Lazio region of central Italy on the Tiber. The original settlement developed on hills facing a ford beside the Tiber Island, the only natural ford of the river in this area. The Rome of the Kings was built on seven hills: the Aventine, Caelian, Capitoline, Esquiline, Palatine, Quirinal and Viminal. The city centre is about 24 kilometres inland from the Tyrrhenian Sea, though the city territory extends to the shore at Ostia.

The Aniene, which flows into the Tiber north of the historic centre, also crosses modern Rome. Vatican City, the smallest country in the world, is an independent country within Rome's municipal boundaries, the only existing example of a country within a city.

Evidence of human occupation of the Rome area goes back approximately 14,000 years. The view that Rome grew from pastoral settlements on the Palatine Hill, above the future Roman Forum, is supported by several excavations. Today there is wide consensus that the city developed gradually through the aggregation of several villages around the largest, on the Palatine, and archaeological evidence places this in the mid-eighth century BCE. The view that Rome was founded deliberately then, as the legend of Romulus suggests, remains a fringe hypothesis.

By 550 BCE Rome was the second largest city in Italy after Taras, with an estimated population of 35,000, though other sources suggest nearly 100,000. When the Republic was founded in 509 BCE the census recorded 130,000, and the city surpassed 300,000 by 150 BCE. After the fall of the Western Empire the city slowly fell under the political control of the Papacy, and in the 8th century it became capital of the Papal States, which lasted until 1870. Rome became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871.

Rome is the capital of Italy and a special municipality named Roma Capitale, with a population of 2.7 million. It hosts the country's principal political institutions and several United Nations agencies, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme. Its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Beginning with Nicholas V (1447 to 1455), almost all popes pursued an architectural and urban programme over four hundred years, and Rome became a major centre of the Renaissance and the birthplace of the Baroque and Neoclassicism. Its first university, La Sapienza, was founded in 1303. In 98 CE, according to Sextus Julius Frontinus, Rome had nine aqueducts feeding 39 monumental fountains and 591 public basins.
ronald-reagan: Ronald Wilson Reagan was born on 6 February 1911 in an apartment in Tampico, Illinois, the younger son of Nelle Clyde Wilson and Jack Reagan. His mother was committed to the Disciples of Christ and led prayer meetings; Reagan credited her spiritual influence. His father focused on making money for the family, a task complicated by his alcoholism. The family lived in several Illinois towns before settling in 1920 in Dixon, where Reagan attended Dixon High School and developed interests in drama and football. He graduated from Eureka College in 1932 with a degree in economics and sociology.

Reagan began as a sports broadcaster in Iowa, and a screen test in 1936 led to a seven-year contract with Warner Bros. Pictures. He arrived in Hollywood in 1937 and made thirty films, mostly B films, before beginning military service in April 1942. His part as George Gipp in Knute Rockne, All American (1940) later led reporters to call him the Gipper while he campaigned for president. He served as an officer in the Army Air Forces, producing over 400 training films, and was discharged on 9 December 1945 as a captain. He began his political life as a Democrat, admiring Franklin D. Roosevelt, and registered as a Republican in 1962 after General Electric dropped him as a speaker.

He was elected governor of California in 1966 and served from 1967 to 1975. He accepted tax increases to balance the budget, and by 1973 the state had a surplus. In 1967 he signed the Mulford Act, which prohibited the public carrying of firearms. After losing the 1976 Republican primaries to President Gerald Ford, he won the nomination in 1980 and defeated President Jimmy Carter. He was inaugurated as the 40th president on 20 January 1981. His economic policy, called Reaganomics, combined deregulation with tax cuts, including the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, and he lifted federal oil and gasoline price controls on 28 January 1981.

Reagan left the presidency on 20 January 1989, at the age of 77, and the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library opened in 1991. He was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 1994, and his capacities gradually deteriorated. He died of pneumonia, complicated by Alzheimer's, at his home in Los Angeles on 5 June 2004. A public funeral was held in the Washington National Cathedral, where Margaret Thatcher, Brian Mulroney, George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush gave eulogies, and he was interred at his presidential library. His tenure is regarded as a realignment toward conservative policies in the United States.
rondonia: Rondônia lies in the North Region of Brazil, bordered by Acre to the west, Amazonas to the north, Mato Grosso to the east and Bolivia to the south. Its capital and largest city, Porto Velho, stands on the Madeira River. The state occupies 237,590 square kilometres and has 52 municipalities. It once held over 200,000 square kilometres of rainforest, and by 2003 about 70,000 square kilometres had been cleared. The area around the Guaporé River belongs to the Beni savanna ecoregion, and the Samuel Dam stands on the Jamari River.

Before the arrival of the Portuguese the region was home to Indigenous peoples speaking Arawan, Chapacuran, Macro-Jê, Nambikwaran, Panoan and Tupian languages and several language isolates. Linguists generally accept that the area of Rondônia is the origin of the Tupian languages. The Spaniard Ñuflo de Chávez was the first European explorer to reach the valley of the Guaporé River, between 1541 and 1542, but only passed through. Bandeirantes came around 1650 to seek gold and other minerals, and Jesuit priests founded the first village. After gold was found on the right bank of the Guaporé, the Portuguese Crown founded the Captaincy of Mato Grosso in 1748.

Its governor, Antonio Rolim de Moura Tavares, named Vila Bela da Santíssima Trindade its capital in 1752 and directed the border demarcation that followed the Treaty of Madrid of 1750. Forts were built on the Guaporé to hold the frontier against the Spanish, the last being Forte Príncipe da Beira, built in 1776. The decline of mining left the region of little economic importance until rubber came to a peak late in the 19th century.

The definitive establishment of Acre in 1903 gave impetus to the region, since the Treaty of Petrópolis obliged Brazil to build the Madeira-Mamoré railway. Decree-Law No. 5812 of 13 September 1943 created the Federal Territory of Guaporé from parts of Amazonas and Mato Grosso, and a law of 17 February 1956 renamed it the Federal Territory of Rondônia in honour of Marshal Cândido Rondon.

Brazil nuts and rubber were the main activities until cassiterite was found. In the 1970s and 1980s tax incentives, federal investment, highways, colonization centres and cheap land drew migrants, largely from the Center-South of Brazil, and in 1982 the territory became a state with 13 municipalities including Porto Velho.

Rondônia has about 1.8 million inhabitants, drawn from all regions of Brazil, with settlers from Paraná, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul prominent. It has 21 Indigenous Territories, the largest being the Uru-Eu-Wau-Wau Indigenous Territory of over 1.8 million hectares. Other cities include Ariquemes, Cacoal, Guajará-Mirim, Ji-Paraná and Vilhena.
ronnie-brunswijk: Ronnie Brunswijk was born on 7 March 1961; his birth village was Moiwana. He joined the Suriname National Army at the age of 18, was considered a good soldier and was sent to Cuba for commando training, after which he was appointed a personal bodyguard of Desi Bouterse. In 1984 he asked for a raise; instead he was discharged on 16 April and refused his back pay. He then sought recognition and rights for the Maroons of the interior, descendants of Africans who had escaped slavery and founded independent communities in the 17th and 18th centuries.

The Surinamese Interior War began at Stolkertsijver on 22 July 1986, when the Jungle Commando captured twelve soldiers guarding a checkpoint. During the war the group received arms and funding from the Netherlands. On 29 November 1986 the Surinamese army attacked Moiwana, murdered at least 39 villagers, mostly women and children, and burned Brunswijk's house; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights later ordered the government to compensate the survivors. The war caused hundreds of deaths and drove more than 10,000 refugees into French Guiana. A ceasefire was negotiated at Kourou on 21 July 1989, and a final peace treaty was signed on 8 August 1992.

A Dutch court in Haarlem convicted Brunswijk in absentia of cocaine smuggling and sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment, reduced to six years on appeal in 2000; he contested the evidence. He chairs the General Liberation and Development Party and has sat in the National Assembly. He owned a gold-mining company, Robruns NV, whose concessions he transferred to a foundation in July 2020 in order to qualify for the vice-presidency.

In the 2020 elections Brunswijk was elected to the National Assembly, and on 29 June 2020 he became its chairman. On 13 July he was elected vice-president by acclamation, with Chan Santokhi as president, and was inaugurated on 16 July. He also owns the football club Inter Moengotapoe and in 2002 built a stadium in Moengo. On 21 September 2021 he played 54 minutes for the club in the CONCACAF League against C.D. Olimpia of Honduras, aged 60 years and 198 days. After a video showed him paying Olimpia players, CONCACAF disqualified both clubs and banned him from its competitions for three years.
rosa-luxemburg: Luxemburg arrived in Zurich in early 1889, when Switzerland was the most important centre of Russian and Polish revolutionary Marxism in exile. She enrolled at the University of Zurich in 1890 and from 1892 studied law, public law and political economy under Julius Wolf. When she reached Germany in 1898 the party was divided by the revisionist controversy, begun by Eduard Bernstein, who argued that many of Marx's predictions were outdated and that the party should become a democratic socialist party of reform.

The Russian Revolution of 1905 shaped her theory of the mass strike, set out in a pamphlet published in 1906. On 4 August 1914 the SPD's Reichstag delegation voted unanimously for war credits. With Karl Liebknecht, Clara Zetkin and Franz Mehring she began to organise an opposition, which became the Spartacus League. She was arrested on 18 February 1915 and spent most of the war in prison, where she wrote the Junius Pamphlet.

In Social Reform or Revolution? (1900) she argued that the struggle for reforms was a means to an end, not an end in itself. In The Accumulation of Capital (1913) she held that capitalism could not realise its surplus value within its own closed system and so had to expand into pre-capitalist spheres, above all in colonies abroad. This drive, in her view, was the economic basis of imperialism and militarism. The Junius Pamphlet called the war an imperialist conflict for which all sides were responsible.

She welcomed the Russian Revolution of 1917 but, in a manuscript written in prison in 1918 and published after her death, condemned the Bolsheviks' suppression of the Constituent Assembly and their abolition of democratic freedoms.

Luxemburg was released from prison on 9 November 1918, during the German Revolution of 1918–1919. With Liebknecht she led the Spartacus League and its daily newspaper, Die Rote Fahne. The Spartacist uprising of January 1919 was not a planned putsch by the KPD, and she at first thought it a mistake, but once the masses were on the streets she urged the workers on. After the Freikorps crushed it, she and Liebknecht were captured and killed.

Her death made her a martyr for revolutionary socialists. After Paul Levi published her manuscript on the Russian Revolution in 1922, Lenin answered with a parable that praised her as an eagle while listing her errors. In Germany she and Liebknecht are honoured each January with a demonstration in Berlin.
rosa-parks: Rosa Louise McCauley was born on 4 February 1913 in Tuskegee, Alabama, the daughter of Leona, a teacher, and James McCauley, a carpenter and mason. As a baby she moved with her mother to Pine Level, Alabama, where she attended the African Methodist Episcopal church, to which she belonged all her life. She completed high school in 1933 with the encouragement of her husband, Raymond Parks, at a time when only 7 per cent of Black people in Alabama held a diploma. In 1941 she began work at Maxwell Air Force Base, which was fully integrated, and said it opened her eyes to an alternative to Jim Crow; on her way home she still had to use segregated buses.

Parks joined the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP in 1943 and served as its secretary. After three attempts between 1943 and 1945 she registered to vote despite measures to disenfranchise Black citizens, and she investigated cases of racial and sexual violence, among them those of Recy Taylor and Jeremiah Reeves. Several women had been arrested before her for keeping their seats on Montgomery buses, including Claudette Colvin, aged fifteen, in March 1955, but activists judged Colvin unsuitable as a test case. After Parks's arrest, E. D. Nixon and Clifford Durr favoured her for her standing in the community and her firm quiet spirit.

She agreed after consulting her family, and the lawyer Fred Gray took her case. The Women's Political Council, led by Jo Ann Robinson, had 35,000 leaflets printed announcing a one-day boycott for 5 December 1955, the day of her trial. After she was found guilty the boycott was extended, and the Montgomery Improvement Association ran a network of transport to sustain it.

Parks and her husband lost their jobs and fell into hardship, and in 1957 they moved to Detroit. She took part in the March on Washington in August 1963, and later supported the Free South Africa Movement. She died on 24 October 2005 aged 92. After a service in Montgomery she lay in state in the United States Capitol rotunda, where 40,000 mourners came, and was buried in Detroit. She received the Spingarn Medal in 1979, the Presidential Medal of Freedom and a Congressional Gold Medal, and was the first Black American memorialised in the National Statuary Hall.
rotterdam: Rotterdam lies in the province of South Holland, in the North Sea mouth of the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta, reached by the New Meuse channel, which was dug to connect first to the Meuse and now to the Rhine. The river Nieuwe Maas divides the city into a northern and a southern part, joined by tunnels and bridges. The Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt give waterway access into the heart of Western Europe, including the industrialised Ruhr, and together with rail and road links they earned the city the nicknames Gateway to Europe and Gateway to the World.

The settlement at the lower end of the fen stream Rotte, then called Rotta from words for muddy water, dates from at least the year 950. Around 1150 large floods ended development and led to the building of protective dikes and dams, including Schieland's High Sea Dike along the northern bank of the Nieuwe Maas. A dam on the Rotte was built in the 13th century, at the present-day Hoogstraat, and in 1340 William IV, Count of Holland, granted Rotterdam city rights.

Rotterdam has always been one of the main centres of Dutch shipping. Its Chamber of the VOC, the world's first multinational, was established in 1602. Since 1795 it has hosted the chief congregation of the liberal Protestant Remonstrants, and its Catholic bishopric dates from 1955. The Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus is counted among its former inhabitants. During the First World War, because of Dutch neutrality and the city's position between Britain, Germany and German-occupied Belgium, it was the world's largest spy centre, and MI6 had its main European office on the Boompjes. On average 25,000 Belgian refugees lived there.

In the early stages of the Second World War the German Luftwaffe bombed the city centre and destroyed many of its older buildings. After an initial crisis of reconstruction the centre became a site of ambitious new architecture. Earlier landmarks include the White House of 1898, the tallest office building in Europe in its day, the Van Nelle Factory of 1929, a monument of modern factory design that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, and Feyenoord's stadium De Kuip of 1936.

Rotterdam is the second-largest city of the Netherlands by population and the largest by area, and it is Europe's largest seaport. It is the centre of the Rotterdam–The Hague metropolitan area, the most populous in the country. Erasmus University Rotterdam is named after Erasmus. The destruction of the city centre in 1940 gave it a varied architectural landscape, with skyscrapers designed by architects such as Rem Koolhaas, Piet Blom and Ben van Berkel.
rouen: Rouen stands on the River Seine in northwestern France and is the prefecture of the region of Normandy and of the department of Seine-Maritime. The Seine has been central to its prosperity: in the Middle Ages the city had a monopoly on river traffic that reached as far upstream as Paris, and today the Port of Rouen is a major axis for maritime cargo.

Rouen was founded by the Gaulish tribe of the Veliocasses, who called it Ratumacos; the Romans called it Rotomagus. It was considered the second city of Gallia Lugdunensis after Lugdunum (Lyon), and under Diocletian it was chief city of Lugdunensis secunda, with an amphitheatre and baths. In the 5th century it became the seat of a bishopric and later a capital of Merovingian Neustria.

The Normans overran it from 841, and in the early 10th century it became the capital of the Duchy of Normandy until William the Conqueror moved his residence to Caen. It received a charter of self-government in 1150. In the 12th century about 6,000 Jews, a fifth of the population, lived in the town, which had a yeshiva known as La Maison Sublime.

On 24 June 1204 Philip II Augustus of France annexed Normandy, and from the 13th century a textile industry based on English wool made the city prosperous. The mayor was assassinated in 1291, Philip IV expelled the Jewish community in 1306, and the Harelle, a revolt of the underclass, in 1389 was suppressed with the loss of the city's charter. Rouen surrendered to Henry V of England on 19 January 1419 after a long siege.

Joan of Arc was burned at the stake there on 30 May 1431, and Charles VII recaptured the city in 1449. It withstood a five-month siege by Henry IV and an English force in 1591/2, and in the Second World War was heavily damaged and its cathedral almost destroyed by Allied bombs.

Rouen is the seat of an archdiocese, with a university and a court of appeal, and its metropolitan area has 715,239 people. Its monuments include Rouen Cathedral, whose Gothic facade Claude Monet painted in a series, the 14th-century astronomical clock known as the Gros Horloge, and the Church of Saint Ouen and the Gothic Church of St Maclou. The Place du Vieux Marché marks the site of Joan of Arc's pyre.
ruhollah-khomeini: Ruhollah Mostafavi Khomeini came from a family of small landowners, clerics and merchants and was born in the town of Khomeyn, in what is now Markazi province. His father was murdered when he was a small child, and his mother and aunt raised him. In 1920 he began studies at the seminary in Arak under Ayatollah Abdolkarim Haeri Yazdi and the following year followed his teacher to Qom, where he studied Islamic law and also philosophy and mysticism. His first political book, Kashf al-Asrar, was published in 1942. He became a marja', a source of emulation, in 1963, after the death of Grand Ayatollah Seyyed Husayn Borujerdi.

In January 1963 Mohammad Reza Shah announced the White Revolution, a programme that included land reform and the enfranchisement of women. Khomeini viewed it as an attack on Islam and on 22 January 1963 issued a declaration denouncing the Shah. On 26 October 1964 he denounced the immunity granted to American military personnel. He was exiled on 4 November 1964, first to Bursa in Turkey and from October 1965 to Najaf in Iraq, where his lectures on the Guardianship of the Jurist were compiled as Islamic Government. In 1978 Saddam Hussein expelled him, and he went to Neauphle-le-Château near Paris.

The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, and Khomeini returned on 1 February to a crowd reported to be as many as five million. On 11 February he appointed Mehdi Bazargan as his own prime minister, in competition with the provisional government of Shapour Bakhtiar. He was de facto head of state until his appointment as supreme leader in December 1979. Iraq invaded in September 1980, and the Iran–Iraq War lasted until August 1988. Khomeini also issued a fatwa calling for the killing of Salman Rushdie, author of The Satanic Verses.

Khomeini died on 3 June 1989 after five heart attacks in ten days. His funeral drew up to 10 million people, and at least ten mourners were trampled to death. In March 1989 he had removed Grand Ayatollah Hussein-Ali Montazeri as his chosen successor after Montazeri criticised the execution of political prisoners. His legacy remains disputed: admirers see a champion of Islamic revival and independence, while critics point to the repression and executions of his rule.
rumi: Rumi's father, Baha ud-Din Walad, was a theologian, jurist and mystic from Wakhsh, where he lived until 1212, when the family moved to Samarkand. The advance of the Mongol armies later forced the family west. After time in various cities of Iran, in Baghdad and in Damascus, Rumi settled in Konya at the age of 19. His name means the Roman, because Anatolia had belonged to the Byzantine empire and was still known as Rum. When his father died, Rumi, aged twenty-five, inherited his position at a madrassa, and he was trained in the Shariah and the Tariqa by Burhan ud-Din Muhaqqiq Termazi until 1240 or 1241. He then began a public life as a jurist, issuing fatwas and preaching in the mosques of Konya.

His meeting with the wandering dervish Shams-e Tabrizi on 15 November 1244 changed his life, turning an accomplished teacher into an ascetic. When Shams disappeared, Rumi grieved deeply, and the verses he composed were collected in the Divan. His scribe and favourite student, Hussam-e Chalabi, suggested that he write a book like those of Sanai and Attar, and Rumi then dictated the six volumes of the Masnavi to him over twelve years.

The Masnavi, or Spiritual Couplets, has about 27,000 lines of rhyming couplets and is often called the Quran in Persian. Many commentators have ranked it first among the mystical poems of world literature. The Divan-i Kabir, named in honour of Shams, holds about 35,000 Persian couplets and 2,000 quatrains, with 90 ghazals and 19 quatrains in Arabic and a few Turkish and Greek couplets.

Rumi's poetry speaks of a love that infuses the world, and he held that the oneness of God is lived most fully through love. He was a Muslim who praised the Quran and held Muhammad to be the most perfect of the prophets, yet traces of religious pluralism run through his work: the lamps are different, he wrote, but the Light is the same.

Rumi fell ill in December 1273 and predicted his own death. His followers founded the Mevlevi order, also known as the whirling dervishes, in 1273. Hussam Chalabi led it until his death in 1284, when Rumi's younger surviving son, Sultan Walad, became grand master, and leadership has stayed in Rumi's family at Konya since. His poetry shaped the Ottoman Turkish, Chagatai, Pashto, Kurdish, Urdu and Bengali literary traditions, and it has been translated into many languages. In 2007 UNESCO took part in celebrating the eight hundredth anniversary of his birth.
rurik-dynasty: Modern scholars consider Rurik a legendary and perhaps entirely fictional figure. The Primary Chronicle, of the early twelfth century, tells of the Calling of the Varangians: tribes at war with one another invited three brothers from overseas to rule them, of whom Rurik settled in Novgorod, Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor in Izborsk. No earlier Kievan source knew of Rurik, and genealogies of the princes usually stopped with Igor of Kiev. Even if Rurik existed, scholars have long doubted or rejected that he was Igor's father.

Before the mid-15th century no source claims that Rurik founded a dynasty. The tradition was set out by churchmen in the 16th century, in the Book of Royal Degrees of 1560 by Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow, which traced the ruling house of Moscow to Rurik and to a supposed kinsman of Augustus Caesar named Prus. For this reason some scholars prefer the name Volodimerovichi, descendants of Volodimer I of Kiev.

The house underwent a major schism after the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054, dividing into branches descended from his sons Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod. By the middle of the twelfth century Kievan Rus' had dissolved into independent principalities, each under a different branch. Vsevolod's line, the Monomakhovichi, named after Vladimir II Monomakh, became predominant. The Olgovichi, descended from Sviatoslav, ruled in Chernigov until the early 14th century. The Romanovichi, the line of Roman the Great, were crowned kings of Galicia and Volhynia and ruled until 1323.

In the north-east the Yurievichi descended from Yuri Dolgorukiy, the founder of Moscow. His great-grandson was Alexander Nevsky, whose son Daniel of Moscow founded the ruling house of Moscow, the Daniilovichi. In all, the house ruled for 21 generations in the male line, a period of more than 700 years. It was briefly revived in Vasili IV of Russia, of the Shuyskiy line, who died without issue. The Time of Troubles lasted until 1613, when Mikhail I founded the Romanov dynasty; his father was descended from the Rurikids through the female line.

Russian and Ukrainian historians have long debated the inheritance of Kievan Rus'. The Russian view treats the Principality of Moscow as its sole heir, resting largely on religious and historical claims. The Ukrainian view of succession, summarised most clearly by Mykhailo Hrushevsky in his History of Ukraine-Rus', is based on continuity through the Kingdom of Ruthenia, Lithuania-Ruthenia and the Cossack Hetmanate. Several branches of the family survive, among them the houses of Shakhovskoy, Gagarin and Lobanov-Rostovsky.
russia: Russia is the largest country in the world, spanning eleven time zones and sharing land borders with fourteen countries. It stretches over the easternmost part of Europe and the northernmost part of Asia, some 9,000 kilometres from east to west, and is one of only three countries bordering three oceans. The Ural Mountains, running north to south through the west, form the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, at 5,642 metres, is the highest peak in Russia and Europe, and Klyuchevskaya Sopka on the Kamchatka Peninsula is the highest active volcano in Eurasia.

Human settlement on Russian territory dates back to the Lower Paleolithic. The East Slavs became prominent in Europe between the 3rd and 8th centuries, and Kievan Rus' was established in the 9th century, adopting Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire in 988. After it disintegrated in the 12th century the Grand Principality of Moscow became the dominant Russian principality and led the unification of Russian lands, culminating in the Tsardom of Russia in 1547. Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721, which became the third-largest empire in history.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 abolished the monarchy and created the Russian SFSR, the first socialist state. After the Russian Civil War it became the principal constituent of the Soviet Union, established in 1922. Amid rapid industrialisation in the 1930s, millions died under Joseph Stalin. The Soviet Union played a decisive role for the Allies on the Eastern Front in World War II, then competed with the United States as a superpower during the Cold War. In 1991 the Russian SFSR emerged from the dissolution of the Soviet Union as the Russian Federation.

Russia had an estimated population of 146 million in 2025, and three-fourths of its people live in urban areas. Moscow is the capital and Saint Petersburg the second-largest city. A constitution adopted after a constitutional crisis in 1993 established a semi-presidential republic. Russian is the official language, and about 81% of the population were ethnic Russians in the 2010 census.
russian-empire: The foundations of a unified Russian state were laid in the 15th century under Ivan III. Moscow became the leading Russian principality, and by the early 16th century the remaining Russian states were united with it. As the only independent Orthodox power after the fall of the Byzantine Empire in 1453, its rulers took symbolic steps towards empire: they married into the Byzantine imperial dynasty, adopted the double-headed eagle and took the title of tsar. Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547. Peter the Great (r. 1682 to 1725) transformed the tsardom into an empire, fought wars that made Russia a major European power, and moved the capital to the newly founded Saint Petersburg.

Catherine the Great came to power in a coup against her husband Peter III and presided over further expansion. Poland was partitioned between 1772 and 1815 and most of its land and population came under Russian rule, and by 1795 Russia was the most populous state in Europe, ahead of France. Alexander I helped defeat Napoleon and established the Holy Alliance. By 1812 Russia had also gained Finland from Sweden, Bessarabia from the Ottoman Empire and some territory in the Caucasus, and it administered Alaska between 1799 and 1867. Most of the empire's growth in the 19th century came from gains in central and eastern Asia.

In 1853 to 1856 Russia fought Britain, France, Sardinia and the Ottoman Empire in the Crimean War; the defeat, formalised in the Treaty of Paris of 1856, forced it to demilitarise the Black Sea. After the 1905 Revolution Nicholas II authorised the State Duma, though ultimate authority remained with him. Russia entered the First World War in 1914 on the side of the Allies; high casualties and shortages of food and fuel led to unrest, and the February Revolution of 1917 brought the abdication of Nicholas II and a Provisional Government, which proclaimed a republic in September.

At its height in the late 19th century the empire covered about 22,800,000 square kilometres, roughly one-sixth of the world's landmass and the third-largest empire in history after the British and Mongol empires. By the 1897 census the population was 126 million, with more than 100 ethnic groups, ethnic Russians making up about 45 per cent. The Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government in the October Revolution, and after winning the Civil War against the Whites established the Soviet Union across most of the former Russian territory.
russian-revolution: The Russian Revolution of 1905 laid the groundwork for 1917. Bloody Sunday triggered nationwide protests and soldier mutinies, and a council of workers, the St. Petersburg Soviet, was created. The revolution was crushed, but it led to the creation of a Duma, which later formed the Provisional Government. Nicholas II was a deeply conservative ruler who believed that his power was granted by Divine Right and, even after 1905 moved him to decree limited civil rights and democratic representation, worked to limit them.

The 1914 Battle of Tannenberg was a disaster for Russia, with over 30,000 troops killed or wounded and 90,000 captured. In autumn 1915 Nicholas took direct command of the army and left his wife Alexandra in charge of the government. Reports of corruption and incompetence spread, and the influence of Grigori Rasputin was widely resented.

On 7 March [O.S. 22 February] 1917 a strike closed the Putilov plant, Petrograd's largest. On International Women's Day women marched to nearby factories and brought out over 50,000 workers, and by 10 March virtually every industrial enterprise in the city was shut. Nicholas abdicated on 15 March [O.S. 2 March], and a provisional government led by the Duma took over. The Petrograd Soviet claimed to represent workers and soldiers, so that Russia had two rival centres of power: the Provisional Government held authority in military and international affairs, the Soviets in domestic matters.

The Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin won support with a programme of peace, land and bread, while the Provisional Government continued the war. The October Revolution began on 7 November [O.S. 25 October], an armed insurrection in Petrograd organised by the Revolutionary Military Committee under Leon Trotsky; its initial assault occurred largely without casualties. The Bolsheviks proclaimed the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic and signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in March 1918.

Many groups did not recognise the Bolshevik government, and Russia fell into a civil war between the Reds and an array of enemies including nationalists, other socialists, anarchists, monarchists and liberals. The Bolsheviks murdered Nicholas II and his family at Yekaterinburg on 16 July 1918. Historians consider the revolutionary period to have ended in 1922 with the defeat of the White Army, and the Soviet Union was formed from the Soviet republics. Historians divide into Soviet-Marxist, Western totalitarian and revisionist schools; the totalitarian school describes a coup by a minority, the revisionists stress the revolution's popular character.
rye: Rye (Secale cereale) belongs to the wheat tribe, Triticeae, which also includes wheat and barley, and is one of several cereals that grow wild in the Levant and central and eastern Turkey. Evidence from the Epipalaeolithic site of Tell Abu Hureyra in northern Syria suggests that rye was among the first cereal crops to be systematically cultivated, around 13,000 years ago, but critics point to inconsistencies in the radiocarbon dates. Domesticated rye occurs in small quantities at a number of Neolithic sites in Anatolia but is otherwise absent from the archaeological record until the Bronze Age of central Europe, around 1800-1500 BCE.

It probably reached Europe as a minor admixture in wheat and was only later cultivated in its own right. Remains have been found in Roman contexts along the Rhine and the Danube and in Britain and Ireland. Pliny the Elder, writing of a grain that may have been rye, called it a very poor food that only served to avert starvation.

Rye is a tall grass, annual or biennial, reaching 1 to 3 metres, with seeds carried in a curved spike. It is much more tolerant of cold and poor soil than other cereals, grows better than any other in heavy clay and light sandy soil, and survives snow cover that would kill winter wheat. It has therefore been especially valuable where the soil is sandy or peaty. Winter rye, sown in autumn, grows again in spring early enough to provide grazing.

Rye is highly susceptible to the ergot fungus. Eating infected rye causes ergotism, with convulsions, miscarriage, necrosis of the digits, hallucinations and death, and damp northern countries that depended on rye were historically subject to periodic epidemics. Modern grain cleaning has practically eliminated it.

Since the Middle Ages rye has been widely cultivated in Central and Eastern Europe, where it is the main bread cereal in most areas east of the France-Germany border and north of Hungary; in Southern Europe it was grown on marginal lands. In Scandinavia it was a staple food in the Middle Ages, and rye crispbread remains popular there. Rye bread, including pumpernickel, is widely eaten in Northern and Eastern Europe. The grain also makes rye beer and rye whiskey, and the drink kvass is fermented from rye bread or flour and malt.

Rye straw is used as livestock bedding, and in Sweden rye flour is boiled with red iron oxide to make the traditional Falun red house paint. In European folklore the Roggenwolf, or rye wolf, is a wolf-shaped field spirit that steals children, and the last heads of grain were often left as a sacrifice to such spirits. The classical scholar Carl A. P. Ruck links these figures with ergot, whose reddish infected grains were known as wolf teeth.
